# AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science

Atharva Naik Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
Email: [arnaik@cs.cmu.edu](mailto:)    Vivek Chari
Affiliation: Microsoft Email: [dfried@cs.cmu.edu](mailto:)    Pol Llado
Affiliation: Microsoft Email: [cprose@cs.cmu.edu](mailto:)    Daniel
Fried Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Carolyn Rosé
Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Benjamin Van Durme
Affiliation: Microsoft    Sam Thomson Affiliation: Microsoft    Justin
Svegliato Affiliation: Microsoft

###### Abstract

Data science agents can automate end-to-end machine learning workflows,
yet they remain far from competitive on human leaderboards. Agents make
process errors such as insufficient exploration, unsound validation,
coding bugs, and poor use of a fixed budget (re-running the same
exploratory data analysis and baseline models in every attempt). We
propose AdaPRA to address these issues: a persistent coding agent
harness that accumulates knowledge across attempts on the same task,
with _rubric-guided process supervision_ that identifies and corrects
errors. Our process reward agent audits the agent’s trajectory and
workspace by executing checks, and adapts its rubrics to each task. We
find that rubrics seeded from easier tasks generalize to harder tasks,
with rubric adaptation further improving performance. With five attempts
per task, AdaPRA improves an 80B Qwen model’s leaderboard percentile by
24.5 points on DSPredict-Easy and 14.8 points on DSPredict-Hard while
reducing process errors. We also show that supervision with rubrics
mined from one base model’s runs improves another (DeepSeek-V3.2), and
that AdaPRA beats DataPRM, a competitive PRM for data science. We also
share our code for reproducibility.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to
caption](2610.33245v1/figures/AdaPRA_Intro_Teaser_No_Rubric_Discovery.png)

Figure 1: AdaPRA corrects process errors. Here, the agent must classify
voice clips into 12 commands. A wrong file path makes every test clip
load as silent audio, so every prediction is classified as the “unknown”
command even though the trajectory indicates no errors. To address this,
AdaPRA checks the predictions file under the _Submission Integrity_
rubric, identifies the cause, and the agent fixes it.

Data science agents can consistently complete end-to-end machine
learning (ML) workflows, yet their scores lag on benchmarks such as
DSGym ([Nie et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)). Much of the gap comes from
_process errors_, mistakes in intermediate steps that lead to worse
outcomes. The most common is _simplicity bias_ [Nie et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib10): agents stop at the first valid pipeline instead of
exploring stronger models, preprocessing, or features. Others include
unsound validation, mismatched training objectives, and leaked
validation sets. Many are silent: the pipeline produces a valid
submission, and the trajectory shows no sign of the error. Agents also
make poor use of repeated attempts: harnesses like DSGym start each
attempt from scratch, so every attempt repeats exploratory data analysis
(EDA), baselines, and strategies that already failed. Competitive
submissions therefore require a harness that accumulates progress across
attempts and _process supervision_ [Lightman et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7)
that corrects process errors, including those that leave no trace in the
trajectory.

We propose AdaPRA, a method with four components: a persistent harness;
a _process reward agent_ (PRA) that supervises the agent; automatic seed
rubric discovery from past agent runs; and task-specific rubric
adaptation. The harness keeps the agent’s workspace across repeated
attempts on the same task, so exploratory insights, and trained models
from one attempt carry into the next. The PRA supervises the agent
during each attempt, judging its trajectory and workspace against
rubrics using tools and code execution [Qiu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12);
[Peng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib11); [Raghavendra et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib13).

We design AdaPRA around five challenges of supervising a long-running
data science agent. First, silent errors leave no trace in the
trajectory, so an LLM judge that reads only the trajectory misses them;
AdaPRA instead runs checks on the agent’s code, outputs, and traces. In
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"),
the agent submits “unknown” for all 158,538 test clips; AdaPRA finds
identical predicted probabilities for every clip, confirms that the code
builds nonexistent paths, and names the fix. Second, the evidence spans
hundreds of turns and a workspace of code, models, and data, too much to
push into the context window, so AdaPRA _pulls_ context on demand.
Third, feedback after an attempt ends comes too late to steer it, so the
PRA reviews at a fixed cadence _during_ the attempt, similar to [Gandhi
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1); at any stage, however, many rubrics are
irrelevant or already passing, so our PRA reports only the relevant
failing ones to avoid flooding the agent’s context. Fourth, rubrics must
target the errors agents actually make, many visible only in the
workspace, so AdaPRA discovers seed rubrics from past agent trajectories
and workspace artifacts, extending the rubric discovery procedure of
[Zhang et al. (2026b)](#bib.bib23). These errors recur across tasks, and
we show that rubrics learned from easier tasks generalize to harder
tasks. Finally, each task has pitfalls that general rubrics cannot
anticipate, so AdaPRA adapts its rubrics to each task as attempts
proceed [Li et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6); [Shao et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14),
which further improves performance.

Replacing the DSGym harness with AdaPRA, using Claude Sonnet-4.6 for the
PRA, improves the mean Kaggle percentile of an 80B Qwen3-Coder-Next
agent by 24.5 points on DSPredict-Easy and by 14.8 points on
DSPredict-Hard, whose tasks span vision, text, speech, and molecular
prediction. These results match or exceed GPT-5.1 with high reasoning
across all metrics. Ablations show that the persistent harness, code
execution, and rubric adaptation each contribute to these gains.

In summary, AdaPRA makes three contributions: (1) a persistent harness
for data science agents that carries progress across attempts, including
EDA findings, baselines, and failed strategies, so that each attempt
spends its fixed budget on new experiments; (2) a PRA that audits the
agent’s trajectory and workspace by executing checks and adapts its
rubrics to each task; and (3) a rubric discovery procedure that
contrasts whole agent attempts, using both their trajectories and
workspace artifacts, to yield seed rubrics that transfer from easier to
harder tasks and to a second base model.

## 2 Related Work

#### Agents for data science.

Agents that automate ML workflows are evaluated on DSGym [Nie et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib10) and agentic data-analysis suites ([Qiu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Kulikov et al., 2026](#bib.bib4), inter alia). ML
engineering agents such as AIDE [Jiang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib3) and
ML-Master [Liu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8) use an external scaffold that
keeps a tree of candidate solutions, picks one to refine, and gives the
model a short, curated context at each step. AdaPRA instead leaves the
search to the coding agent: its harness keeps the workspace across
attempts, and the agent decides what to reuse, using files as memory [Xu
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib20); [Zhou et al. (2026)](#bib.bib24). The two
designs could be combined, with such a scaffold running over a
persistent agent.

#### Rubric adaptation.

Prior work has explored rubrics, checklists, and natural-language
principles as reward specifications that are more flexible than scalar
preference labels [Wang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib17); [Gunjal et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib2); [Viswanathan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib16); [Yu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib21) (compared in detail in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Rubric and Principle Reward Models ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Other work adapts rubrics over time: RubricEM [Li et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib6) adds and prunes criteria in an evolving buffer
through a meta-RL training loop, turning past attempts into reusable
experience, and [Shao et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14) evolve rubrics during
training to mitigate reward hacking. These papers adapt rubrics to shape
a training reward and apply them with a standard LLM judge that has no
tools or code execution. AdaPRA instead adapts rubrics while it
supervises the agent on the task at hand, without gold feedback such as
Kaggle scores: the PRA checks rubrics with tools and code, and a
per-task store turns pitfalls that a general rubric set cannot cover
into explicit criteria for later reviews of the same task.

#### Process reward agents.

Process reward models (PRMs) score intermediate steps rather than only
final outcomes [Lightman et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7); [Gandhi et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib1). _Process reward agents_ (PRAs) extend PRMs to verify
actively before judging, by executing code, retrieving evidence, or
exploring a workspace, in math [Zhang et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib22),
software engineering [Raghavendra et al. (2026)](#bib.bib13), GUIs
[Xiong et al. (2025)](#bib.bib19), medical reasoning [Sohn et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib15), data analysis [Qiu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12), and
general reward modeling [Peng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib11). Code execution
makes verification more grounded, but existing PRAs rely on a static
rubric set, whereas AdaPRA audits both the trajectory and the workspace
of a long-running agent and adapts its rubrics to each task.
Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Appendix A Design Coverage of Related Systems ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Design Coverage of Related Systems ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
summarizes the design coverage of related systems.

#### Rubric discovery.

Rubrics can be discovered automatically from past agent behavior.
RubricEM discovers rubrics through policy decomposition across training
episodes [Li et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6), and [Zhang et al.
(2026b)](#bib.bib23) refine per-prompt rubrics for RL post-training by
contrasting the two highest-scoring candidate responses to a prompt.
Both derive rubrics from responses or trajectories alone, whereas we
also mine the workspace artifacts each attempt leaves behind
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
and show that the resulting rubrics transfer from easier to harder
tasks.

## 3 Method

![Refer to caption](2610.33245v1/figures/AdaPRA_method_v3_j.png)

Figure 2: AdaPRA overview. The agent works in a workspace that persists
across attempts. During each attempt, the PRA reads the trajectory and
workspace, runs check scripts in its own workspace, injects feedback on
failing rubrics into the agent’s trajectory, and adds, updates, or
retires rubrics in the per-task store.

AdaPRA
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
combines a persistent harness
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Agent Harness with Memory ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
with a PRA that checks the agent against rubrics discovered offline
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
grounds its judgments in code
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Process Reward Agent ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
and adapts the rubrics to each task
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Adaptive Rubrics ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

### 3.1 Problem Setup

Let $`x`$ be a predictive data science task represented as a set of
files and a natural-language prompt. In each attempt, the base agent
produces a trajectory $`\tau=(a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{T},o_{T})`$ of
actions $`a_{t}`$ (writing code, training models, creating submissions)
and observations $`o_{t}`$ (logs, scores, errors), and operates in a
workspace $`W`$ on the file system. The agent makes $`N`$ attempts per
task, each ending with a submission file, and every condition we
compare, including the baselines, makes the same $`N`$ attempts
(§[4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
We score every attempt on Kaggle only to compute evaluation metrics, and
neither the agent nor the PRA ever sees these scores, test labels, or
any other external feedback between attempts.

Process errors such as simplicity bias and leaky cross-validation often
still yield a valid submission
(Table [10](#A10.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
so we supervise the process with $`m`$ rubrics
$`\mathcal{R}=\{\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{m}\}`$, natural-language criteria
such as _“compare the first valid baseline against at least one stronger
model family.”_ Every $`c`$ base-agent turns and when the base agent
tries to finish, the PRA scores the partial trajectory
$`\tau_{:t}=(a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t},o_{t})`$ up to the current turn
$`t`$ and the current workspace against each rubric $`\rho_{j}`$,

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       S(x,W,\tau_{:t},\rho_{j})=(p_{j},i_{j},e_{j},\hat{a}_{j}),
       ```                                                         |     |

with probability of satisfaction $`p_{j}\in[0,1]`$, importance
$`i_{j}\in[0,1]`$, rationale $`e_{j}`$, and suggested next action
$`\hat{a}_{j}`$. The probability of satisfaction $`p_{j}`$ captures the
confidence that the agent adhered to the rubric guidelines. The
importance $`i_{j}`$ captures the relevance of the rubric to task $`x`$
and to the current stage $`t`$ of the attempt, since one rubric set
serves many kinds of task and some rubrics apply only at later stages
(e.g., a rubric requiring a prediction file applies only once a model
has been trained).

We show the agent only the relevant failing rubrics, those with
$`i_{j}\geq 0.5`$ and $`p_{j}<0.6`$
(Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model inference settings. ‣ Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
i.e., rubrics with importance at least 0.5 and a greater than 40% chance
of having failed.¹¹ 1 We show only failures because in an earlier
version that reported every rubric, most rubrics passed in nearly every
report and the agent’s next action was similar whether or not a report
contained a failure
(Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Feedback Content in an Earlier Version ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The PRA compiles these rubrics into a natural-language report and
injects it directly into the message stream of the agent
(Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Process Reward Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).²²
2 During development, we found this more effective than writing the
report to a markdown file that the agent could choose to open and
inspect, but sometimes did not despite instructions in its system
prompt.

### 3.2 Agent Harness with Memory

In our harness, the agent acts through a terminal and a file editor and
is built on OpenHands [Wang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib18). The DSGym
harness [Nie et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10) resembles a REPL and resets the
workspace between attempts, so each attempt rebuilds data loading,
validation, and a baseline from scratch. Our harness keeps one workspace
per task across all $`N`$ attempts: exploratory notes, features, trained
models, validation results, and submissions from attempt $`k`$ remain
available in attempt $`k{+}1`$, and only the model context resets. This
lets later attempts avoid or fix errors from earlier ones and spend
their budget on directions earlier ones left open. Each later attempt
also receives the agent’s own summaries of all earlier attempts, so it
can explore new directions with awareness of what has already been
tried. In supervised conditions, each summary is followed by the
feedback from the final review of that attempt
(Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Base Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Everything carried across attempts is produced by the agent or the PRA,
and the only scores it contains are the agent’s own validation scores.
Turn, wall-clock, and per-command limits bound each attempt
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

### 3.3 Rubric Discovery

Hand-writing rubrics requires expert effort that becomes infeasible
across many tasks and trajectories of hundreds of turns. We discover
rubrics offline from past harness-only runs of the base agent, using the
leaderboard percentile of each attempt to contrast stronger and weaker
attempts
(Figure [3](#A9.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science");
prompts in
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Like RubricEM [Li et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6), we derive rubrics from
agent trajectories, but we also mine the workspace each attempt leaves
behind (code, notes, and submissions). From [Zhang et al.
(2026b)](#bib.bib23), we borrow contrastive discovery and the principle
that rubrics be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE).
In stage one, an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6) extracts generalizable
behaviors that plausibly drove each attempt’s outcome, either _good
behaviors_ or _issues_, each with quoted evidence. It is told whether
the attempt ranks in the top or bottom quarter of the attempts on the
same task, so each attempt is judged relative to its siblings and task
difficulty is held fixed
(Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
In stage two, a single LLM call clusters the behaviors into a MECE
rubric set, with good behaviors and issues as positive and negative
evidence for the same rubric. Stage one extracts both kinds from every
attempt, but to keep the behaviors that explain the score gap, we
cluster only the good behaviors of top attempts and the issues of bottom
attempts (519 of 906;
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

#### Evidence source.

Some behaviors are visible only in the files left behind (e.g., code and
markdown notes) and others only in how the agent worked, as recorded in
the trajectory, $`\tau`$. The judge therefore sees $`\tau`$, a snapshot
of the workspace $`W`$, and the agent’s end-of-attempt summary, and tags
each rubric by the evidence it needs. Artifact-grounded rubrics can be
checked from $`W`$ alone (“the submission has the correct columns and
row count”). Trajectory-grounded rubrics require $`\tau`$ (“kept
retrying the same failing command”). The tags measure what each view
contributes to discovery.

#### Discovered set.

On harness-only runs of DSPredict-Easy (38 tasks, 5 attempts each),
stage one mines 906 behaviors, 564 issues and 342 good behaviors. Issues
are mostly trajectory-grounded (344 of 564) and good behaviors mostly
artifact-grounded (235 of 342), so mining only the trajectory would
under-represent good behaviors, and a judge that sees only the workspace
would miss most issues. Stage two yields 17 rubrics covering validation,
model exploration and selection, preprocessing, submission integrity,
and efficiency, including criteria with no artifact counterpart, such as
pivoting to a qualitatively different approach once repeated experiments
stop improving. Together with two cross-attempt rubrics
(Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
these form the 19 seed rubrics
(Table [10](#A10.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
used in every configuration and applied unchanged to DSPredict-Hard.

### 3.4 Process Reward Agent

Judging many of these errors requires reviewing the modeling code
itself: whether a stronger model family was trained and compared,
whether the cross-validation leaks information, whether engineered
features reach the final model, and whether the submission comes from
the pipeline the agent reports. The trajectory records the agent’s
claims, which can mislead a judge that takes them at face value, so the
PRA is itself an agent, with its own terminal and scratch space that
checks the claims against the workspace $`W`$ (instructions and tools in
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Process Reward Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
For each rubric, the PRA can write and execute its own code in its own
workspace against the base agent’s files (e.g. recompute a
cross-validation score from out-of-fold predictions) and ground
$`p_{j}`$ in the result. Rubrics that need no computation, such as the
trajectory-grounded “kept retrying the same failing command”
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
it scores by reading the trajectory or files. The base agent’s workspace
is read-only to the PRA, so supervision cannot alter the base agent’s
work.

The fixed cadence delivers feedback while a course correction is still
possible, similar to [Gandhi et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1)
(Appendix [N](#A14 "Appendix N PRA Cadence ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
varies $`c`$), and the finish review acts as a final gate. Trajectories
reach hundreds of turns, so instead of being injected into the PRA’s
context, $`\tau_{:t}`$ and the transcript of each earlier attempt are
written as turn-annotated text files to the PRA’s workspace, which the
PRA opens and searches with its tools (file names in
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Process Reward Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The PRA reads them selectively, and initial experiments showed that this
on-demand access works better than appending each new batch of agent
turns to the PRA’s context
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Supervision Design Choices ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The base agent is paused while the PRA runs, and this wall-clock time
does not count against its budget. Failing rubrics
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Problem Setup ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
are returned to the agent ordered by importance, with their suggested
fixes, to keep feedback short and actionable
(Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M Example PRA Feedback ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
shows examples). If the finish review fails, the agent gets one final
refinement round, which bounds the cost of the gate.

### 3.5 Adaptive Rubrics

The seed rubrics from
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
capture failures that recur across tasks, but each task has pitfalls of
its own. The PRA can therefore add, update, and retire rubrics in a
per-task store (similar to RubricEM [Li et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6)),
initialized with the seed set and kept across the task’s attempts, so a
failure found in one attempt becomes an explicit criterion in later
reviews. The PRA edits the store with three tools. _Add_ creates a
rubric only after the PRA has run and recorded a check for it in the
same review, _update_ rewrites a rubric’s specification, and _retire_
deactivates a rubric and records the reason. Stores are isolated across
tasks, so that results do not depend on the order in which tasks are
run. Added rubrics tend to be task specific. For example, on House
Prices the PRA added a rubric it named _prediction underdispersion_,
which checks whether out-of-fold predictions are much less spread out
than the target, a sign that the model pulls extreme prices toward the
mean.

## 4 Experiments

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate on DSGym’s [Nie et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10) DSPredict-Easy,
38 mostly tabular Kaggle competitions from the Playground Series, and
DSPredict-Hard, 54 competitions spanning tabular, vision, text, audio,
and molecular data. Because the seed rubrics are discovered on
DSPredict-Easy
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
it serves as the development benchmark and DSPredict-Hard as a held-out
test of transfer to harder tasks.

#### Models and budget.

The base agent is Qwen3-Coder-Next, an 80B open-weights coding model,
and the PRA uses Claude Sonnet 4.6. Every condition makes $`N=5`$
attempts per task, and all conditions built on our harness share the
same per-attempt limits
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
DSPredict-Hard attempts receive a larger budget and GPU access because
its tasks involve larger data and neural models.

#### Baselines and Ablations.

On each benchmark we compare six conditions. Two baselines are without
process supervision: the DSGym harness [Nie et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10),
which resets the workspace between attempts, and our persistent harness
without AdaPRA supervision (_harness only_), which isolates the effect
of our persistent harness. To compare with competitive PRMs, we replace
the PRA with DataPRM [Qiu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12), a 4B generative
process reward model that runs code to verify each agent step and scores
the step 1 (correct), 0.5 (minor issues), or 0 (fatal error); the base
agent, harness, and feedback channel are those of AdaPRA
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F DataPRM Baseline ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Both supervisors execute code and score the agent, but DataPRM judges
each step’s correctness without rubrics, while AdaPRA checks the
trajectory and workspace against seed and task-adapted rubrics that also
cover errors spanning many steps, such as stopping at the first valid
pipeline. The remaining three conditions share our harness and the seed
rubrics: AdaPRA; _$`-`$adaptive rubrics_, which keeps the seed set
fixed, so on DSPredict-Hard it measures how well the seed rubrics alone
transfer; and _$`-`$PRA_, which keeps adaptation but removes the PRA’s
terminal, so it can read files but not run code
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Process Reward Agent ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"),
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Process Reward Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
As external context we also report the single-attempt DSGym results of
Qwen3-Coder-480B and GPT-5.1 (high) [Nie et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10).

#### Additional ablations.

To isolate the effect of supervision within an attempt, we run two
further ablations on DSPredict-Easy with a single attempt per task: the
PRA cadence, $`c\in\{5,10,20\}`$ agent turns
(Appendix [N](#A14 "Appendix N PRA Cadence ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
and DeepSeek-V3.2 as the base agent in place of Qwen3-Coder-Next
(Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Alternative Base Agent ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

#### Metrics.

We report four task-level rates: Pct., the mean leaderboard percentile
(private leaderboard where one exists, else public); Valid, the share of
tasks with a submission Kaggle accepts and scores; \>Median, the share
of tasks scoring above the leaderboard median; and Medal, the share of
tasks reaching a Kaggle medal threshold. Averaging only over tasks with
a valid submission would favor a condition that fails to submit on hard
tasks, because it drops its lowest scores; all rates therefore divide by
every task in the benchmark and count an invalid or missing submission
as a zero percentile. Ideally, a deployed system would identify the best
submission without test scores, so we evaluate four selection policies
(Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Selection-Policy Analysis ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")):
the first attempt, the last attempt, the mean over attempts (the
expected result of choosing one at random), and the best attempt, an
oracle upper bound. The main tables report the best and mean attempts.
We test each difference in mean percentile for significance with a
one-sided paired permutation test over tasks, which randomly swaps the
two conditions’ scores within each task
(Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

on the 54 competitions of DSPredict-Hard (fixed denominator of 54 tasks,

is also –, and their rates are shown as published

### 5.1 DSPredict-Easy

AdaPRA raises the mean percentile of Qwen3-Coder-Next from 44.5 in the
DSGym harness to 69.0 and the above-median rate from 50.0% to 86.8%
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Every task receives a valid submission, as does every individual
attempt. Over our harness alone (_harness only_), AdaPRA adds 8.2
percentage points and 15.7 above-median points; the percentile gain is
significant ($`p<0.001`$,
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The gain holds per attempt (61.0 vs. 51.3 mean percentile), so
supervision improves typical attempts as well as the best one. A single
AdaPRA attempt on average matches a single GPT-5.1 (high) attempt in the
DSGym harness (61.0 vs. 60.4 mean percentile). Because the seed rubrics
were discovered on DSPredict-Easy, DSPredict-Hard is the cleaner test of
AdaPRA.

### 5.2 DSPredict-Hard

On DSPredict-Hard, AdaPRA raises the mean percentile from 21.3 to 36.1,
the valid rate from 68.5% to 90.7%, and the above-median rate from 11.1%
to 33.3%
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Over our harness alone, it adds 10.6 percentage points ($`p<0.001`$) and
14.8 above-median points. AdaPRA’s best attempt exceeds a single GPT-5.1
(high) attempt on valid, above-median, and medal rates. Per attempt,
AdaPRA exceeds GPT-5.1 in valid and above-median rates (86.3 vs. 85.7
and 24.1 vs. 14.3) but trails it slightly in medal rate (4.1 vs. 4.8).

### 5.3 Ablations

#### Harness.

Our harness alone (persistent workspace and terminal-based tools) lifts
the base agent on both benchmarks, raising the mean percentile from 44.5
to 60.8 and the valid rate from 76.3% to 100% on DSPredict-Easy, and
from 21.3 to 25.5 and 68.5% to 81.5% on DSPredict-Hard. The two
components split the gain differently: the harness contributes 16.3
percentage points and supervision 8.2 on DSPredict-Easy, versus 4.2 and
10.6 on DSPredict-Hard. Our harness is enough to produce valid and
reasonable pipelines on easier tasks, while harder tasks need
supervision.

#### Adaptive rubrics.

Freezing the seed rubrics lowers the mean percentile by 1.7 points on
DSPredict-Easy and by 4.3 points on DSPredict-Hard, where it also cuts
the above-median rate from 33.3% to 22.2%. The Hard gap is significant
($`p=0.024`$; 32 wins, 13 losses).
§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Easy-to-Hard Generalization ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
shows why adaptation matters more on DSPredict-Hard: its tasks have more
domain-specific pitfalls that the seed set cannot anticipate. The PRA
adapts almost entirely by adding rubrics (177 additions, one update, and
no retirements across the four adaptive runs), mostly in the first two
attempts
(Figures [4](#A12.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
and [5](#A12.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
in
Appendix [L](#A12 "Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Code execution changes what it adds: prediction-sanity rubrics, which
compute statistics of the agent’s predictions such as their dispersion
relative to the target, make up 35% (DSPredict-Easy) and 19%
(DSPredict-Hard) of additions with execution and 3% and 7% without it
(Table [18](#A12.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

#### PRA.

Scoring rubrics by reading alone lowers the mean percentile from 69.0 to
63.0 on DSPredict-Easy and from 36.1 to 31.8 on DSPredict-Hard, along
with the Easy medal rate (7.9% to 2.6%) and the Hard above-median rate
(33.3% to 25.9%). The gap is significant on DSPredict-Easy ($`p=0.012`$)
but not on DSPredict-Hard ($`p=0.077`$; 29 wins, 18 losses). Without
code execution ($`-`$PRA), supervision still improves on the harness
alone on both benchmarks (63.0 vs. 60.8 and 31.8 vs. 25.5), so rubric
feedback helps even without execution. It gets a higher Hard medal rate
(9.3% vs. 5.6%, five medals vs. three) despite a lower mean percentile,
which we attribute to the noisiness of the metric: a medal depends on
whether a submission’s rank crosses a fixed leaderboard cutoff, so small
score differences can flip it, especially on dense leaderboards.

AdaPRA has the highest mean percentile on both benchmarks and the
highest above-median rate on DSPredict-Hard (33.3% vs. 22.2% and 25.9%;
all three tie at 86.8% on DSPredict-Easy), so code execution and rubric
adaptation are complementary.

#### Additional analyses.

Cadence
(Appendix [N](#A14 "Appendix N PRA Cadence ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")):
with a single attempt per task, every cadence we test improves on the
harness alone (48.4 mean percentile), and invoking the PRA every 10
turns works best (56.4). Invoking it more often ($`c{=}5`$, 52.7) or
less often ($`c{=}20`$, 49.9) gives smaller gains, consistent with a
trade-off between timely feedback and interrupting the agent. We
therefore use $`c{=}10`$ on DSPredict-Easy. On DSPredict-Hard we use
$`c{=}20`$ to bound cost: Hard attempts take 1.6 times as many agent
turns
(Table [21](#A16.T21 "Table 21 ‣ Appendix P Agent and PRA Turns ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
and the PRA already accounts for 75% of the cost of a Hard run
(Table [22](#A17.T22 "Table 22 ‣ Appendix Q Run Costs ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Base agent
(Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Alternative Base Agent ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")):
with DeepSeek-V3.2 as the base agent and one attempt per task, AdaPRA
raises the mean percentile from 36.9 to 44.7 and the above-median rate
from 23.7% to 47.4% over the harness alone. It wins on 25 tasks and
loses on 11 ($`p=0.005`$), so rubrics discovered from Qwen3-Coder-Next’s
runs also help a second base model.

### 5.4 Easy-to-Hard Generalization

The seed rubrics are discovered only on DSPredict-Easy, whose tasks are
mostly tabular, yet they improve DSPredict-Hard, whose tasks span
vision, text, audio, time series, and molecular data. With the seed
rubrics frozen, supervision adds 6.3 percentage points over the harness
alone on DSPredict-Hard ($`p=0.007`$), close to its 6.5-point gain on
DSPredict-Easy ($`p=0.017`$).

The same process failures occur on both benchmarks in the frozen-rubric
runs, which score the same 19 rubrics throughout
(Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Seed Rubric Failures Across Benchmarks ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Every seed rubric fails in at least 24% of DSPredict-Hard attempts, so
none is specific to easy tasks. For each rubric we compute two
statistics per benchmark: its mean importance over all PRA reviews and
its failure rate, the share of attempts in which it fails at least once.
Ranking the 19 rubrics by either statistic gives nearly the same order
on both benchmarks (Spearman $`\rho=0.91`$ for importance, $`\rho=0.66`$
with $`p=0.002`$ for failure rate). The most frequent failures on both
benchmarks are the two simplicity-bias rubrics, too little model
diversity and ensembling and repeating near-identical experiments
without pivoting (68–84% of attempts). Harder tasks add pipeline
failures that the seed set already covers: invalid cross-validation
rises from 32% to 57% of attempts and unverified submissions from 33% to
52%. Simplicity bias and pipeline errors are properties of the agent,
which persist across domains, so rubrics that target them transfer.
Table [17](#A11.T17 "Table 17 ‣ Examples of transferred rubrics. ‣ Appendix K Seed Rubric Failures Across Benchmarks ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Seed Rubric Failures Across Benchmarks ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
shows seven such cases, each a failure on a non-tabular DSPredict-Hard
task that a DSPredict-Easy rubric flagged and the agent fixed within the
same attempt.

Adaptation covers what the seed set misses. The PRA adds 0.8 rubrics per
task on DSPredict-Easy and 1.2 on DSPredict-Hard, and adds at least one
on 79% of Hard tasks versus 51% of Easy tasks
(Figure [6](#A12.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Hard additions encode domain knowledge absent from tabular tasks, such
as non-negative time-to-failure predictions in LANL Earthquake
Prediction and excluding quantum-mechanical sub-components of the target
from the features in CHAMPS Scalar Coupling. The seed set transfers the
domain-general failures and adaptation supplies the domain-specific
ones, consistent with the larger adaptation gain on DSPredict-Hard.

## 6 Conclusion

We propose AdaPRA, which combines a harness whose persistent workspace
accumulates knowledge across attempts on a task, a process reward agent
that audits the agent’s trajectory and workspace by executing checks and
adapts its rubrics to each task, and offline discovery of seed rubrics
from agent trajectories and workspace artifacts. With Qwen3-Coder-Next
as the base agent, AdaPRA raises the mean Kaggle percentile from 44.5 to
69.0 on DSPredict-Easy and from 21.3 to 36.1 on DSPredict-Hard, matching
or exceeding GPT-5.1 (high). The harness, the process reward agent, and
adaptive rubrics each contribute to the gain, and removing any one of
them lowers performance on both benchmarks. Rubrics discovered on mostly
tabular tasks (DSPredict-Easy) transfer to vision, text, audio, and
molecular tasks (DSPredict-Hard) because the process failures they
target come from the agent rather than the domain, and adaptation adds
the domain-specific criteria that a general rubric set does not cover.
Supervision with rubrics mined from Qwen3-Coder-Next’s runs also
improves a second base model (DeepSeek-V3.2), and AdaPRA outperforms
DataPRM [Qiu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12), a competitive PRM proposed in
prior work.

## 7 Future Work

First, training the base agent on dense feedback from the PRA could let
it internalize the process criteria and depend less on supervision at
test time. Second, the PRA adapts rubrics without measuring how each
affects the outcome and never retired one in our runs; assigning credit
to individual rubrics could better inform adaptation. Third, training
smaller open-weight models to replace the closed-source PRA would extend
[Gandhi et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1) from non-agentic critics to agentic
PRAs. Finally, harness evolution like Meta-Harness [Lee et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib5) could further improve our persistent harness.

## Limitations

Supervision cadence. To bound compute and API cost, we invoke the PRA
every 20 turns on DSPredict-Hard instead of the 10 turns that work best
on DSPredict-Easy; the PRA already accounts for 75% of the cost of a
Hard run
(Table [22](#A17.T22 "Table 22 ‣ Appendix Q Run Costs ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
in
Appendix [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q Run Costs ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
On DSPredict-Easy, a cadence of 20 is the weakest setting we test
(Appendix [N](#A14 "Appendix N PRA Cadence ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
so the DSPredict-Hard results may understate the gains of more frequent
supervision.

Benchmark coverage. We evaluate only on DSGym’s DSPredict-Easy and
DSPredict-Hard. Both consist of Kaggle competitions scored on a
leaderboard metric, so we do not test whether rubric-based supervision
helps in other data science settings, such as open-ended analysis or
tasks without a predictive objective.

Number of attempts. All multi-attempt results use five attempts per
task, and the additional ablations use a single attempt. We do not study
how the gains of supervision change as the number of attempts grows,
where selecting among more unsupervised attempts may recover part of the
difference.

Rubric adaptation. Adaptation almost only adds rubrics (177 additions,
one update, and no retirements;
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Ablations ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
so the rubric store grows over a run. The PRA does not attribute local
validation gains to individual rubrics, so it has little signal for
revising or retiring rubrics that do not help. Better credit assignment
could make adaptation more selective.

Models. Our main results use a single base agent (Qwen3-Coder-Next) and
a single PRA model. We test a second base agent, DeepSeek-V3.2, only
with one attempt per task on DSPredict-Easy
(Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Alternative Base Agent ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

Reproducibility. The PRA uses Claude Sonnet 4.6, a closed model accessed
through a commercial API. Exact reproduction depends on the model
remaining available and unchanged, and its retirement or updates could
change results.
