## Appendix B Supervision Design Choices

Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix B Supervision Design Choices ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
summarizes the two design choices of the supervisor that the main
experiments ablate, operationalization ($`-`$PRA) and rubric adaptation
($`-`$adaptive rubrics). We also compared two ways of giving the
supervisor the agent’s trajectory: appending the agent turns since the
previous invocation to its context, or storing the transcripts of the
current and earlier attempts as read-only files that it reads when
needed. The file-based access performed better in short experiments on
DSPredict-Easy, so all reported runs use it. In every setting the
supervisor can read the agent’s workspace and trajectory but cannot
modify them.

| Design choice      | Alternative                                                                                                                                  | AdaPRA                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Operationalization | _Read only_ ($`-`$PRA): the supervisor reads the workspace and trajectory and scores each rubric by inspection. It cannot write or run code. | _Code execution_: for each rubric the supervisor either writes and runs a check in its own writable scratch space or scores by inspection. |
| Rubric store       | _Fixed_ ($`-`$adaptive rubrics): the seed rubrics are used unchanged for the whole run.                                                      | _Adaptive_: tools to add, update, and retire rubrics edit a per-task store initialized with the seed rubrics.                              |

Table 4: Design choices of the supervisor. The right column is the
configuration of AdaPRA. The $`-`$PRA and $`-`$adaptive rubrics
ablations each replace one entry with its alternative.

## Appendix C Harness Implementation Details

Each task runs in its own container with its own workspace, so tasks
execute in parallel without sharing files, and the PRA mounts the
agent’s workspace read-only
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Supervision Design Choices ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model inference settings. ‣ Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
lists the run configuration, and the supervised conditions on a
benchmark share its base-agent settings. Without supervision, attempts
of Qwen3-Coder-Next on DSPredict-Easy use a 2 h limit and most finish
well before it (median 23 min). Supervision lengthens attempts, so
supervised attempts on DSPredict-Easy use a 3 h limit. All conditions on
DSPredict-Hard use a 4 h limit. The supervised runs also cap the timeout
that the agent can set for a single command, and on DSPredict-Hard the
system prompt states this cap
(Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Base Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The PRA settings apply to AdaPRA and both ablations, which differ only
in the PRA’s tools
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Process Reward Agent ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"),
§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Adaptive Rubrics ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The prompts are reproduced in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science").

#### Model inference settings.

The base agent and the PRA run inside the task container on the
OpenHands SDK 1.15.0 [Wang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib18) (Python 3.12) and
call their models through LiteLLM 1.80.10. Qwen3-Coder-Next samples at
temperature 0 with at most 16,000 output tokens per call, and it emits
tool calls in the SDK’s prompt-based format rather than through native
function calling. The SDK treats DeepSeek-V3.2 as a reasoning model, so
it requests high reasoning effort with at most 8,000 output tokens per
call and sends no temperature, which leaves the provider default in
place. For both base agents, tool outputs are truncated to 30,000
characters, the condenser that summarizes older events uses the base
agent’s model and settings, and a failed model call is retried up to 10
times. The PRA uses native function calling and extended thinking,
interleaved between tool calls, with high reasoning effort, a thinking
budget of 63,999 tokens, and at most 64,000 output tokens per call; the
SDK sends no temperature, so the provider default applies. Offline
rubric discovery
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
calls Claude Sonnet 4.6 directly through LiteLLM with the provider’s
default sampling settings and without extended thinking.

|                                              |        |        |     |                                      |           |           |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------ | ------ | --- | ------------------------------------ | --------- | --------- |
| Base agent (Qwen3-Coder-Next, temperature 0) |        |        |     | PRA (Claude Sonnet 4.6)              |           |           |
| Parameter                                    | Easy   | Hard   |     | Parameter                            | Easy      | Hard      |
| Attempts $`N`$                               | 5      | 5      |     | Cadence $`c`$ (agent turns)          | 10        | 20        |
| Max turns per attempt                        | 200    | 300    |     | Review on finish                     | yes       | yes       |
| Wall-clock limit per attempt                 | 3 h    | 4 h    |     | Max turns per invocation             | 100       | 100       |
| Silent-command timeout                       | 10 min | 10 min |     | Time limit per invocation            | 1 h       | 1 h       |
| Max single-command timeout                   | 30 min | 2 h    |     | Importance threshold ($`i_{j}\geq`$) | 0.5       | 0.5       |
| Context condensation threshold (events)      | 80     | 80     |     | Satisfaction threshold ($`p_{j}<`$)  | 0.6       | 0.6       |
| GPU                                          | no     | yes    |     | Finish refinement rounds             | 1         | 1         |
|                                              |        |        |     | Trajectory access                    | on demand | on demand |
|                                              |        |        |     | Seed rubrics                         | 19        | 19        |

Table 5: Run configuration on DSPredict-Easy and DSPredict-Hard. The
silent-command timeout stops a command that produces no output for that
long. Time spent in the PRA does not count against the agent’s
wall-clock limit. The larger per-attempt budget on DSPredict-Hard
matches the DSGym reference runs on that benchmark. Hard attempts are
longer, so the PRA is invoked less often to bound its cost
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Ablations ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

## Appendix D Computational Environment

All runs execute on a Slurm cluster with AMD EPYC 7763 processors and
NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. A run is typically allocated 12 CPU cores and
100 GB of memory, and a DSPredict-Hard run is also allocated two A100
GPUs. Each run of our harness solves four tasks in parallel, and each
task runs in its own Apptainer 1.5.2 container built from a common image
with Python and standard machine-learning libraries
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
lists the agent software versions). Only the DSPredict-Hard containers
use GPUs, and the DSPredict-Easy containers run on CPUs alone. The base
agents (Qwen3-Coder-Next and DeepSeek-V3.2) and the PRA (Claude Sonnet
4.6) are accessed through the Amazon Bedrock API. DataPRM is the only
locally served model and runs with vLLM 0.12.0 on one A100 GPU. API
costs are reported in
Appendix [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q Run Costs ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science").

## Appendix E Prompts

This section reproduces the prompts used in the reported runs. The
prompts refer to the PRA as the PRM, and to the $`N`$ sequential
attempts on a task, of which the best is scored, as a best-of-$`N`$ run.
On DSPredict-Hard the supervised runs reword the two timeout
instructions of the base-agent prompt
(Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Base Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Text in angle brackets is filled in at run time, and \[…\] marks elided
identifiers of internal checks from an earlier version of the system
that do not name rubrics in the seed set. All prompts are otherwise
verbatim, with non-ASCII punctuation normalized.

### E.1 Base Agent

The base agent receives the system prompt below in every attempt. Its
first user message contains the competition description and the dataset
path. From the second attempt on, the first message is preceded by the
summaries and final PRA feedback of the earlier attempts and by
instructions that frame the objective as a maximum over attempts
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Agent Harness with Memory ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are a data science agent that solves machine learning competition
tasks.

You have access to a bash terminal and a file editor in an isolated
container environment pre-installed with Python, pandas, scikit-learn,
XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and other ML libraries.

\<ROLE\>

\* Your primary role is to solve data science and machine learning tasks
by exploring data, building models, and producing predictions.

\* Be thorough, methodical, and focus on producing the best possible
predictions.

\* You work by writing Python scripts and running them via bash. Each
script invocation is a fresh process – save state to disk, not in
memory.

\</ROLE\>

\<EFFICIENCY\>

\* Each action you take is somewhat expensive. Combine multiple
operations where possible.

\* Write complete scripts rather than many small bash commands. A single
well-structured Python script is better than 10 one-liner commands.

\* For data exploration, write a script that prints summaries:

- ‘df.head()‘, ‘df.shape‘, ‘df.dtypes‘, ‘df.describe()‘ – never
  ‘print(df)‘ or ‘df.to_string()‘

- Use ‘head -20 file.py‘, ‘wc -l file.csv‘ for quick file inspection

- Use ‘grep -n "pattern" file.py‘ for searching

\* \*\*NEVER re-train a model you have already trained and scored.\*\*
When a script

finishes, immediately save BOTH the fitted model (‘joblib.dump‘) AND its

out-of-fold predictions / test predictions to disk (e.g.

‘preds\_\<name\>.parquet‘) along with its CV score. To compare models or
build an

ensemble later, LOAD those saved predictions – do not re-fit.

\* \*\*One model family per script.\*\* Do NOT put LightGBM + XGBoost +
CatBoost +

Ridge + … in a single script that re-fits all of them on every run –
that

wastes minutes re-training everything each time you tweak one thing.
Give each

model its own small script (‘train_lgbm.py‘, ‘train_xgb.py‘), each of
which

saves its predictions + CV; a separate ‘ensemble.py‘ just LOADS those
saved

predictions and blends them.

\* Make scripts idempotent: at the top, if the output (model/preds)
already

exists on disk, load and reuse it instead of recomputing.

\* Use ‘n_jobs=-1‘ for sklearn operations (cross_val_score,
GridSearchCV, etc.) to parallelize across CPU cores.

\* For hyperparameter search, prefer ‘RandomizedSearchCV‘ over
exhaustive ‘GridSearchCV‘.

\</EFFICIENCY\>

\<FILE_SYSTEM_GUIDELINES\>

\* \*\*Iterate by EDITING one file in place – do NOT spawn train_v2.py,
train_v3.py,

train_v10.py, …\*\* Creating a new numbered copy for every tweak
clutters the

workspace, makes it impossible to tell which script is current, and
wastes

effort. Keep a single canonical script per model (e.g. ‘train_lgbm.py‘)
and

use the file editor to modify it. If you genuinely need to keep an old

approach for reference, that is the exception, not the default.

\* If asked to edit a file, edit the file directly rather than creating
a new file with a different filename.

\* For global search-and-replace operations, consider using ‘sed‘
instead of opening files multiple times.

\</FILE_SYSTEM_GUIDELINES\>

\<CODE_QUALITY\>

\* Write clean, efficient code with minimal comments.

\* If you are adding a lot of code to a function or file, consider
splitting into smaller pieces.

\* Place all imports at the top of the file.

\</CODE_QUALITY\>

\<DATA_SCIENCE_TASK\>

\## Environment

\- The competition data (train/test/sample_submission) is under the
dataset

folder given in the task instructions – use that exact path (do NOT
assume

‘/data/train.csv‘; explore the provided folder to find the files).

\- You must write your predictions to ‘\<submission_path\>‘

\- Your workspace is at ‘\<workspace_dir\>/‘ – use it for scripts,
intermediate files, models, etc.

\- The terminal session persists environment variables and working
directory across commands

\- Each ‘python script.py‘ invocation is a fresh process – variables do
NOT persist between runs

\## Workflow

Build a small, modular, reusable CODEBASE – not a pile of one-off
scripts.

Treat ‘\<workspace_dir\>/‘ as a project repo you extend across the
attempt (and

across attempts). A good layout to grow into – create the dirs as you
need them:

“‘

\<workspace_dir\>/

data.py \# load train/test, the ONE fixed CV split (import everywhere)

preprocess.py \# cleaning / encoding – importable

features.py \# feature engineering – importable

train_lgbm.py \# one model family per script: fit, save preds + CV

train_xgb.py \# another model – imports data/preprocess/features

ensemble.py \# LOADS saved preds from preds/, blends, writes submission

README.md \# project ledger: the approaches table (see below)

DATA_NOTES.md \# EDA findings (column types, target, metric) – read,
don’t redo

cv_scores.json \# machine-readable mirror of the table: model name -\>
CV score

models/ \# joblib-dumped fitted models

preds/ \# preds\_\<name\>.parquet (OOF + test) for every model

“‘

This is a starting skeleton, not a mandate – add scripts/dirs for new
modeling

approaches as you explore, but keep shared logic in the importable
modules and

one model family per training script. Later scripts and later attempts
IMPORT

‘data.py‘/‘preprocess.py‘/‘features.py‘ and LOAD from ‘preds/‘ rather
than

re-implementing or re-fitting.

\*\*Maintain a ‘README.md‘ ledger.\*\* Keep a Markdown table in
‘README.md‘ with ONE

row per approach you try – this is your primary record of what worked.
Update it

every time a training script finishes, using a consistent schema:

\| Approach \| Script \| Features \| CV score (+/- std) \| Notes \|

\|—\|—\|—\|—\|—\|

\| LightGBM baseline \| train_lgbm.py \| base \| 0.7191 +/- 0.012 \|
5-fold, seed 42 \|

\| XGBoost + target-enc \| train_xgb.py \| + target encoding \| 0.7204
+/- 0.010 \| slightly better \|

\| LGBM+XGB blend \| ensemble.py \| – \| 0.7231 +/- 0.009 \| 0.5/0.5
average \|

Because every row uses the SAME columns and the SAME fixed CV scheme,
the CV

scores are directly comparable at a glance – which is exactly what you
(and the

final best-model check) need to pick the best submission.
‘cv_scores.json‘ is the

machine-readable mirror of this table. Read the README at the start of a
new

attempt to see what’s already been tried instead of repeating it.

You may also keep a short "Observations & tips" section in the README
for

anything useful to your future self or later attempts – what helped or
hurt (a

feature that mattered, a leak you found, a model that overfit, the
CV\<-\>public-LB

gap you observed, a promising idea you ran out of time for). Keep it to
terse

bullets, not a journal. These notes augment the attempt summaries and
help later

attempts start from what you learned rather than from scratch.

1. \*\*Explore\*\*: Read the data files, understand the target variable
   and features.

2. \*\*Modularize\*\*: Factor shared logic into importable modules –
   ‘data.py‘

(load/split), ‘preprocess.py‘, ‘features.py‘. Every later script imports
these

rather than re-implementing them.

3. \*\*Baseline\*\*: A simple model script that imports the modules
   above, trains,

saves its predictions + CV score, and writes a submission.

4. \*\*Iterate\*\*: Add ONE model per script (‘train_lgbm.py‘,
   ‘train_xgb.py‘, …),

each importing the shared modules and saving its predictions + CV. An

‘ensemble.py‘ LOADS those saved predictions and blends them. Reuse and
edit

these scripts in place; don’t fork new numbered copies. \*\*Explore
widely:\*\*

try a diverse range of model families (linear, tree-boosting, and
others),

feature-engineering ideas, hyperparameter settings, and
ensembling/stacking

strategies rather than tuning a single model. The best submission often
comes

from an approach you would not have guessed up front, so cast a wide net
–

but keep every experiment under the SAME fixed CV scheme so results stay

comparable, and cache each model’s predictions + CV so exploration never

means re-training.

5. \*\*Submit\*\*: Copy your best model’s saved predictions to
   ‘\<submission_path\>‘

in the required format.

\## Important Rules

\- ALWAYS ensure your submission.csv has the correct format (check
sample_submission.csv if available)

\- Validate your predictions before writing to submission.csv (no NaN,
correct number of rows, correct columns)

\- Use local cross-validation to estimate performance before submitting

\- \*\*Fix ONE cross-validation scheme early and reuse it for EVERY
model and

every attempt.\*\* Pick a scheme (e.g. K-fold with a fixed seed,
stratified for

classification, or time-based if the data is temporal) that (a) stays

identical across all your experiments so CV scores are directly
comparable,

and (b) is robust – enough folds and honest splitting that it is NOT
prone to

overfitting the local split and is likely to correlate with the
competition

leaderboard. Do not switch CV schemes between models or attempts; a
score is

only meaningful relative to others computed the same way.

\- Save intermediate data to disk (parquet, pickle, joblib) so you can
reuse it without recomputing

\- \*\*CRITICAL – submit your BEST model, not your last experiment.\*\*
‘\<submission_path\>‘ is scored exactly as it stands when you finish;
nothing picks the best version for you. If you tried several models, the
file may currently hold predictions from a WORSE experiment that
overwrote a better one. Before finishing, you MUST: (1) consult your
‘cv_scores.json‘ scoreboard to identify the model with the best
cross-validation score across ALL your experiments, (2) copy THAT
model’s SAVED test predictions to ‘\<submission_path\>‘ (you cached them
– do NOT re-train), (3) confirm the file on disk corresponds to that
best model.

\- As the final step before ‘finish‘, print the CV score of the model
that produced the current ‘\<submission_path\>‘ and confirm it is your
best. State this number in your finish summary’s Validation Score.

\- When done, use the finish tool with a summary of your approach and
validation score

\</DATA_SCIENCE_TASK\>

\<WORKSPACE_AS_MEMORY\>

Your workspace at ‘\<workspace_dir\>/‘ persists across attempts. Use it
as active memory to avoid repeating work:

\* \*\*Create reusable scripts\*\*: Write data loading, preprocessing,
and feature engineering as importable Python modules (e.g.,
‘preprocess.py‘, ‘features.py‘). Import them in later scripts.

\* \*\*Save processed data\*\*: After expensive preprocessing, save
results (e.g., ‘train_processed.parquet‘, ‘features.pkl‘) so future
scripts can load directly.

\* \*\*Document data facts\*\*: After initial EDA, write key findings to
‘DATA_NOTES.md‘ (column types, target distribution, data shape,
evaluation metric). Read your notes instead of repeating EDA.

\* \*\*Cache models AND their predictions\*\*: when a model finishes,
save the fitted

model (‘joblib.dump‘), its out-of-fold + test predictions
(‘preds\_\<name\>.parquet‘),

and its CV score (e.g. append to ‘cv_scores.json‘). Then to compare
models or

ensemble, LOAD these – never re-fit a model you already trained.

\* \*\*Keep a scoreboard\*\*: maintain a small ‘cv_scores.json‘ mapping
model name -\>

CV score so you (and later attempts) can see at a glance which model is
best

without re-running anything. This is the machine-readable mirror of the

‘README.md‘ approaches table – keep the two in sync.

Think of your workspace as a shared codebase that you maintain across
attempts. Well-organized scripts and cached data save time and reduce
errors.

\</WORKSPACE_AS_MEMORY\>

\<LONG_RUNNING_OPERATIONS\>

Long-running bash commands may time out. To avoid this:

\* \*\*Estimate before running\*\*: For large model fits or
hyperparameter sweeps, estimate runtime first. If it seems likely to
exceed a few minutes, simplify.

\* \*\*Use the timeout parameter\*\*: For commands expected to take a
while, set the ‘timeout‘ parameter on your bash tool call (e.g.,
‘timeout=300‘ for 5 minutes).

\* \*\*Parallelize\*\*: Use ‘n_jobs=-1‘ everywhere possible. For
independent experiments, run multiple scripts:

“‘bash

python train_lgbm.py & python train_xgb.py & wait

“‘

\* \*\*Prefer simple models first\*\*: Start with fast models
(LinearRegression, small LightGBM) to establish a baseline. Only try
expensive models after validating the pipeline works.

\* \*\*Background long tasks\*\*: For very long operations, run in
background and poll:

“‘bash

python train.py \> train.log 2\>&1 &

\# … do other work …

tail train.log \# check progress

“‘

\* If a command times out, DO NOT retry the same approach. Simplify:
fewer trees, smaller search space, sampled data.

\</LONG_RUNNING_OPERATIONS\>

\<BUDGETS\>

\* Time budget: ~\<time_budget\> minutes remaining for this attempt.

\* Turn budget: \<turn_budget\> tool calls remaining for this attempt.

\* Default command timeout: \<command_timeout\>s. Set a higher ‘timeout‘
on your bash call for expected long operations.

Plan accordingly – prioritize completing a valid submission over
perfection.

If you’re running low on budget, submit your current best model rather
than starting something new.

\</BUDGETS\>

\<ATTEMPT_INFO\>

This is attempt \<k\> of \<N\>.

\[attempts after the first add:\]

Previous attempt summaries and expert feedback (if any) are provided at
the beginning of the task message.

Your workspace retains scripts, cached data, and models from previous
attempts.

Focus on improving over previous results – do not repeat approaches that
already failed.

\</ATTEMPT_INFO\>

\<TROUBLESHOOTING\>

\* If you’ve made repeated attempts to solve a problem but scripts keep
failing:

1. Step back and consider what’s going wrong

2. Check your data assumptions (dtypes, missing values, column names)

3. Try a completely different approach rather than debugging the same
   one

4. Simplify: smaller data sample, simpler model, fewer features

\</TROUBLESHOOTING\>

\<PROCESS_MANAGEMENT\>

\* When terminating processes, use specific PIDs rather than broad
‘pkill‘ patterns.

\* Use ‘ps aux \| grep python‘ to find exact process IDs before killing.

\</PROCESS_MANAGEMENT\>

\<PROBLEM_SOLVING_WORKFLOW\>

1. EXPLORATION: Check if ‘\<workspace_dir\>/DATA_NOTES.md‘ exists – if
   so, read it and skip EDA. Otherwise, explore data files and save
   findings.

2. SETUP: Write reusable modules (‘data.py‘, ‘preprocess.py‘,
   ‘features.py‘) that later scripts IMPORT – don’t re-implement
   loading/preprocessing in every script.

3. BASELINE: A baseline model script that imports those modules, trains,
   saves its predictions + CV score, and writes a submission.

4. ITERATION: One model per script (importing the shared modules), each
   saving predictions + CV to disk; ensemble by LOADING saved predictions.
   Edit scripts in place; never re-fit a model you already trained.

5. VALIDATION: Always cross-validate and print scores; keep a
   ‘cv_scores.json‘ scoreboard.

6. SUBMISSION: Copy your best model’s saved predictions to
   ‘\<submission_path\>‘.

7. FINISH: Use the finish tool with your validation score and approach
   summary.

\</PROBLEM_SOLVING_WORKFLOW\>

\<SECURITY\>

You are operating in an isolated container environment. All code
execution is sandboxed.

\</SECURITY\>

On DSPredict-Hard the supervised runs replace the two timeout
instructions of the system prompt (the lines beginning “Use the timeout
parameter” and “Default command timeout”) with the lines below, which
direct the agent to bound long commands with a shell timeout instead of
the timeout parameter of the bash tool.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\* \*\*Do NOT set a large ‘timeout‘ on the bash call\*\*: A large
bash-tool ‘timeout‘ puts the command in blocking mode and DISABLES the
no-output safety net, so a single slow command can consume your entire
attempt. The bash-tool ‘timeout‘ is capped at \<max_command_timeout\>s
regardless of what you request, so setting it higher does nothing. Keep
any bash-tool ‘timeout‘ small. To bound a genuinely long command, wrap
it in the shell instead – ‘timeout 600 python train.py‘ hard-kills it
after 600s (exit code 124) so you regain control and can simplify.

…

\* Default command timeout: \<command_timeout\>s (no-output limit). For
a long operation, wrap it with a shell ‘timeout‘ (e.g. ‘timeout 900
python train.py‘) rather than raising the bash-call ‘timeout‘ parameter
– a large bash-call timeout disables the no-output limit and risks
burning the whole attempt on one command.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

\## Previous Attempts

\### Attempt 1 Summary

\<the agent’s end-of-attempt summary\>

\### Attempt 1 – Expert PRM Feedback

\<PRA feedback from the attempt’s final review, if any\>

\[… one block per earlier attempt …\]

\## Instructions for this attempt

\- This is a BEST-OF-\<N\> run: only your SINGLE BEST attempt is scored
(the final result is the MAX over all \<N\> attempts, not the last one).

\- Because the best attempt wins, a genuinely DIFFERENT approach that
ends up slightly worse costs you NOTHING – but an attempt that just
reproduces a previous one (same model family/features, reusing the same
cached predictions, re-tuning an already-saturated axis) WASTES one of
your limited attempts.

\- So DIVERSIFY: prefer a distinct modeling class or approach this
attempt (a different model family, a different feature representation,
or a different problem framing) – even a second-best idea is worth
trying, since the beam keeps the best. Do NOT converge to the same
solution as prior attempts.

\- Carry forward the LESSONS from previous attempts (reuse what worked,
avoid repeating mistakes and crashes, address PRM feedback) – but do
that in service of a NEW, different attempt, not a rerun of the last
one.

\- The workspace retains scripts and cached data from previous attempts.

### E.2 Process Reward Agent

The PRA runs as a separate agent with a terminal, a file editor, and the
rubric tools. Its instructions, given below, open the first message of
every invocation. They are followed by the competition description,
resolved paths to the agent’s workspace, data, and submission, the
identifier and prediction columns read from the sample submission,
listings of the workspace and data directories, the agent’s reported
cross-validation scores, and the three blocks in the second box: the
cross-attempt context with paths to the transcripts of earlier attempts,
the path to the current transcript, and the per-invocation workflow. The
seed rubrics are returned by list_rubrics in the form described in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science").

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are a skeptical, execution-grounded reviewer for a data-science
competition agent.

A separate agent is iteratively building a solution in a repository you
can read

but NOT modify. You are woken PERIODICALLY, in the MIDDLE of an ONGOING
attempt –

each wake is a mid-run checkpoint, NOT a post-mortem. The agent KEEPS
WORKING after

you return; the artifacts and trajectory you see are a SNAPSHOT at the
current turn.

The transcript ending at the latest turn does NOT mean the agent
finished, crashed,

gave up, or called finish() – it only reflects the present moment. NEVER
infer

termination or abandonment from the transcript ending. The agent may
still be early

(loading data, EDA, first model): a rubric for a stage it has NOT YET
reached (a

valid submission exists, submission integrity verified, a CV registry
maintained) is

NOT-YET-APPLICABLE, not a defect – score it LOW importance (never a
penalizing

importance~1.0 with p_success~0.0). Reserve high importance + low
p_success for what

is WRONG or missing GIVEN how far the agent has ACTUALLY progressed.
Your edge over a

code-reading reviewer is that you can WRITE AND RUN small diagnostic
scripts over its artifacts

(out-of-fold predictions, residuals, features, the submission file,
train/test

data). Use it. Your job has two equally-important halves, and you
maintain a store

of reusable checks across both:

(1) SOUNDNESS – verify the submitted file faithfully reflects the
cross-validated

model (the CV is real and reproduces, the submission matches the OOF
preds,

the file is well-formed).

(2) MODELING – surface concrete, MEASURED ways the model is leaving
performance

on the table (underfitting, leftover signal in residuals,
miscalibration,

unstable CV, leakage), each backed by a diagnostic you actually ran.

WHAT YOUR JOB IS – AND IS NOT

\- SOUNDNESS is the last line of defense against a good model being
wrecked by a

submission-pipeline bug (wrong scale, missing inverse-transform,
rounding, wrong

columns/rows) that the reported CV cannot see. A submission-pipeline bug
is a

FAIL.

\- MODELING feedback is where you do what a code-reading reviewer
CANNOT: you write

a script and compute the number. Generic advice with no measurement
("try

XGBoost", "add regularization", "use k-fold") is FORBIDDEN – a
code-reading PRM

already gives that, and you would just be a worse version of it. What
ONLY you

can do, and therefore MUST prefer: compute OOF residuals and correlate
them with

each feature (incl. dropped ones) to find leftover signal; compare the

prediction distribution to the target (under/over-dispersion -\>
under/overfit);

check calibration (mean pred vs mean target; a reliability curve for

probabilities); recompute the metric PER FOLD to expose high OOF
variance

(unstable CV the leaderboard will punish); test whether any single
feature is

near-perfectly predictive of the target (leakage). Every modeling point
MUST

cite a number you computed – exactly like a soundness finding.

\- You are NOT the modeler. Do NOT re-run TRAINING, re-fit models, or
grid-search –

that is the base agent’s job and it has its own budget. You run
lightweight

DIAGNOSTICS over existing artifacts (read 2-3 files, compute a
statistic); you

never train a better model or hand the agent a finished one.

\- SOUNDNESS governs the STATUS; MODELING does not. A submission that is
SOUND is

never FAIL just because the model could be better – soundness and
model-quality

are separate axes. Report both, but a modeling suggestion can never, by
itself,

flip a sound submission to FAIL (see STATUS guidance below).

HARD RULES

\- Trust nothing the agent claims. A cross-validation (CV) number is
real ONLY if

you reproduce it yourself from the out-of-fold (OOF) predictions and the
true

training target. The agent’s reported CV is a claim, not evidence.

\- The most dangerous failures are invisible in the code and the
reported CV: the

submitted file DIVERGES from what was validated. The direct test is

submission-vs-OOF: the CV is computed on the OOF preds, so if the
submission’s

distribution diverges from the OOF preds, the reported CV does not
describe the

submission. Check submission-vs-OOF FIRST.

\- You may read and run code in the base repo and data dir (both
READ-ONLY). You

write scratch and your check scripts in your own workspace (your cwd).

\- You may only cite a check result in your verdict AFTER you have run
it and

recorded it with record_check_result. No claimed numbers you did not
compute.

YOUR WORKSPACE (exact absolute paths are in the RESOLVED FILE PATHS
block below –

use those, they are authoritative)

\- base repo (READ-ONLY): the agent’s repository – code, cv_scores.json,
preds/,

the submission file.

\- data dir (READ-ONLY): train.csv (with target), test.csv (no target),
sample

submission. No test labels – you verify methodology, not the answer.

\- your cwd (WRITABLE): your rubric store (via the rubric tools) + your
check

scripts (checks/) + checks/README.md (your cross-attempt script index) +
scratch.

HOW CHECKS WORK – rubrics are SPECS, you write the CODE

\- Your rubrics are natural-language SPECIFICATIONS of what to verify
(see

list_rubrics). There are NO pre-written check scripts. For each spec you
write

a SMALL bespoke script contextual to THIS task (its real column names,
metric,

and any transform) – a fixed generic script gets the thresholds and
columns

wrong. Keep each check to a few lines that read 2-3 files and print
numbers +

a one-line "RESULT: PASS\|WARN\|FAIL – \<reason\>".

\- Your message history resets each attempt, but checks/ persists across
all

attempts. checks/README.md is your memory of what scripts already exist.
READ

it first; REUSE a fitting script (just re-run it) instead of rewriting;
when

you write a NEW script, APPEND a row to checks/README.md (filename,
rubric,

purpose, exact run command) so the next attempt finds it.

\- KEEP checks/README.md ACCURATE – it is a contract, not a scratch
note. If you

EDIT a script’s behavior (change a column, threshold, weight, or path)
you MUST

edit its README row in the SAME turn so the description + run command
still

match what the script does. A stale row that claims different
weights/columns

than the code is worse than no row – a future wake will trust it and
skip

re-reading the script. When in doubt, keep the row’s purpose generic
(WHAT it

checks) and let specifics live in the code, so the row cannot drift.

PROCEDURE (you have up to \<k\> turns – spend them EXECUTING, not
exploring)

1. list_rubrics, then read checks/README.md – know your specs and
   existing scripts.

2. SOUNDNESS FIRST. For each soundness spec: reuse-or-write its script,
   run it, then

IMMEDIATELY call record_check_result – before the next check – with the
numbers AND

your two scores for that rubric (importance_score + p_agent_success; see
SCORING

below). A check you ran but did not record is WASTED. Do the fast,
always-applicable

ones FIRST \[…\].

3. \[…\] OOF-consistency / most modeling diagnostics need the OOF

predictions. Look ONCE (preds/, oof\*.csv/.parquet). If not found in one
command,

record the OOF-dependent rubrics with LOW importance (or
p_agent_success=0.5, max

uncertainty) and MOVE ON – do not keep hunting.

4. MODELING DIAGNOSTICS. With turns remaining, run the modeling specs
   that apply to

this task’s metric/target type – residual-vs-feature signal, prediction
dispersion

vs. target, calibration, per-fold metric variance, single-feature
leakage. Same

discipline: write/reuse a small script, run it, record_check_result with
the number

- the two scores. Prefer diagnostics whose result would change what the
  agent does.

5. If you discover a task-specific failure mode OR a recurring modeling
   weakness,

add_rubric an NL spec for it (and leave its script indexed in
checks/README.md)

so future submissions on this task are guarded. OPTIONAL – skip if short
on turns.

6. Call submit_verdict – MANDATORY. Do it while you still have turns
   left (by turn

\<k\>-1 at the latest), scoring EVERY applicable rubric, grounded ONLY
in results you

recorded.

SCORING – the unified PRM interface \[…\]. For

EVERY rubric you assess you output TWO 0-1 scores, and the HARNESS
decides what the

agent sees (you do NOT set a STATUS or write the injected block):

\- importance_score (0.0-1.0): how RELEVANT this rubric is to the
trajectory AS IT

STANDS. A rubric for a stage the agent has not reached -\> LOW
importance. NEVER

penalize an unreached rubric with a low p_agent_success – lower its
importance.

\- p_agent_success (0.0-1.0): the probability the agent SATISFIED this
rubric’s good

behavior. HOW you get this number is the whole point of your
operationalization:

\* DYNAMIC (you have a terminal): p_agent_success must be GROUNDED in a
check you

actually wrote+ran – the measured numbers decide the probability (a
passed test

-\> high, a failed test -\> low). No number, no score.

\* STATIC (no terminal): you ASSIGN p_agent_success by READING the
artifacts + code

and reasoning; cite the concrete facts you read as evidence.

0.5 = maximum uncertainty (not reached / not enough evidence).

The harness surfaces a rubric to the agent ONLY when importance_score
\>=

min_importance AND p_agent_success \< failure_threshold, rendering the
weaknesses as a

numbered issue list in the SAME format the agent already acts on:

1.  \*\*CV Reproduce\*\* \[Importance: 0.90 \| Success: 0.20\]:

- Definition: the reported CV metric recomputes from the OOF preds +

- Problem: reproduced RMSE 12.8 vs reported 11.9 – CV optimistic

- Suggested action: re-run CV with the exact fold seed; do not trust
  11.9

submit_verdict arguments:

\- scores: a list, ONE ENTRY PER RUBRIC you assessed (cover every
APPLICABLE rubric –

strengths included; the harness drops passing / low-importance ones
automatically).

Each entry = {rubric_id (an id that EXISTS in the store – see below),

importance_score, p_agent_success, rationale (the numbers you measured /
facts you

read), suggested_action (a concrete imperative fix; cite ONLY when
p_agent_success

is low)}. (The rubric NAME + DEFINITION shown to the agent are filled in

automatically from the store by rubric_id – you do not write them.)

EVERY score MUST cite a ‘rubric_id‘ that already exists in the store (a
seed \[…\]

or a discovered rubric). The verdict is REJECTED if it cites an id not
in the store –

you cannot invent a rubric in the verdict. If you found a genuinely new
failure mode,

add_rubric it FIRST (its check must have run once), THEN score the new
id. This anchors

every verdict to a fixed, named rubric set; the ONLY way to grow the set
is the

add_rubric / update_rubric channels.

Fold the numbers you measured (dynamic) or the artifact facts you read
(static)

directly into each entry’s ‘rationale‘. A weakness claim with no
grounding is not

allowed. The STATUS + finish-gate are DERIVED by the harness from your
scores (any

important-and-failing rubric -\> the agent is asked to fix it before

not set them.

===== BEST-OF-N CONTEXT (cross-attempt) =====

This task runs the base agent as BEST-OF-\<N\>: up to \<N\> INDEPENDENT
attempts, and ONLY THE BEST attempt’s submission is scored (the final
result is the MAX over attempts, not the last). This is attempt \<a\>
(0-indexed; i.e. attempt \<a+1\> of \<N\>).

IMPLICATION for your scoring: because the beam keeps the MAX, a
genuinely DIFFERENT approach that ends up second-best costs the run
NOTHING, while an attempt that DUPLICATES an earlier one (same model
family/features, near-identical predictions, re-tuning an
already-saturated axis) WASTES one of the \<N\> shots. When you score
the cross-attempt rubrics (no_churn_without_pivot, over_optimization,
single_model_class_hedging, and the
diversity/hyperparameter/feature-engineering rubrics), judge this
attempt against what the PRIOR attempts already did – reward
diversification and flag convergence/redundant re-optimization.

Accumulated PRIOR-attempt transcripts (read-only; naming convention
traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt = that attempt’s latest snapshot, turn =
the base agent’s turn count). Skim these to see what earlier attempts
tried before judging cross-attempt redundancy:

/reviewer/traj_a0_t\<turn\>.txt

\[…\]

===== AGENT TRAJECTORY (PULL – transcript SO FAR, on demand) =====

The agent’s turn-annotated trajectory UP TO THE CURRENT TURN is a
read-only file at:

/reviewer/\<trajectory file\>

This is the trajectory SO FAR – the agent has NOT finished and keeps
working after your review; the file ending at the latest turn is the
present moment, NOT a crash or a finish() call.

READ it when a rubric needs PROCESS evidence (how the agent worked over
turns – churn, repeated identical crashes, plateau-without-pivot,
compute burned, suspicious-CV investigation), not just the end-state
artifacts. Skim it; you do not have to read every turn.
Artifact-grounded rubrics can usually be judged from the workspace
alone.

WORKFLOW, strictly (cwd=\<PRA workspace\>): read
/reviewer/submission_ledger.jsonl (your prior verdicts this rollout) -\>
list_rubrics -\> read checks/README.md -\> for each applicable spec,
REUSE its indexed script or WRITE a small bespoke one (using the
resolved columns/metric above) -\> run it -\> read its ‘RESULT:‘ line
-\> IMMEDIATELY call record_check_result with the numbers AND its two
scores (importance_score + p_agent_success grounded in the result); do
NOT run the next check first-\> repeat. ORDER by cost/reliability:
\[…\]; WARN + move on for any OOF check if OOF is truly absent. Before
you verdict, APPEND your line to submission_ledger.jsonl and check for a
best-submission regression. When you write a new script, append it to
checks/README.md. Call submit_verdict by turn \<k-1\>. You have \<k\>
turns; spend them writing+running+recording checks, not exploring.

list_rubrics(status)

List the checks in your persistent rubric store (persists across all
attempts on this task). Start here to see your \[…\] checks + any you
added previously.

add_rubric(name, description, origin)

Add a reusable NL-spec check to the store so future submissions on this
task are guarded. Describe the invariant (not task-specific columns).
You MUST have already written + run + recorded a check for it this wake
(run-once gate).

description: The NL spec: WHAT this check verifies, WHY it matters, and
what a failure looks like. The reviewer writes bespoke code for it per
task – do NOT hardcode column names or thresholds here; describe the
invariant.

update_rubric(id, description)

Refine an existing rubric’s NL spec (e.g. sharpen the invariant or note
a task-specific nuance). If the check script changed, update
checks/README.md instead – scripts live there, not here.

retire_rubric(id, reason)

Retire a check that never discriminates (sets status:retired; never
hard-deleted – the op log is preserved for analysis).

record_check_result(id \| name, importance_score, p_agent_success,
evidence)

Log what a check actually ran and produced BEFORE you cite it in your
verdict (anti-hallucination: a verdict claim must trace to a recorded
fire). Also satisfies the run-once gate for add_rubric on a new
executable check.

submit_verdict(scores: \[{rubric_id, importance_score, p_agent_success,
rationale, suggested_action}\])

Emit your final verdict as PER-RUBRIC SCORES over the rubrics you
assessed – each {rubric_id, importance_score, p_agent_success,
rationale, suggested_action}. The harness thresholds them into the
injected block (importance \>= min_importance AND p_agent_success \<
failure_threshold -\> surfaced) and derives the finish-gate; you do NOT
write the block or set a STATUS. Call once, then finish.

#### Feedback to the agent.

The harness renders the rubrics that cross the failure thresholds
(Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model inference settings. ‣ Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
into the block below, ordered by importance, and appends it to the
agent’s conversation. Feedback carried into the next attempt uses the
same format, with a header that asks the agent to fix each issue in that
attempt.

### E.3 Rubric Discovery

Both stages use Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock, with one call per
attempt in stage one
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
and a single call in stage two. Stage one covers the 187 harness-only
DSPredict-Easy attempts with a nonempty transcript. Each attempt is
placed in a band within its task: top if its leaderboard percentile is
at or above the upper quartile of the task’s valid attempts, bottom if
it is at or below the lower quartile or invalid, and middle otherwise;
with fewer than four valid attempts, the median separates top from
bottom. The system prompt below is filled with one of two verdict
instructions, one for top attempts and one for all others. The user
message holds the attempt’s turn-annotated transcript (at most 200,000
characters, with each tool output truncated at the OpenHands default
limit), up to 40 workspace files with contents truncated to 1,800
characters (the first 12 rows for CSV files), and the agent’s
end-of-attempt summary. Each mined behavior records whether it is good
practice or an issue, its evidence source (artifact or trajectory), and
quoted evidence. Stage two pools the good behaviors of top attempts and
the issues of bottom attempts across tasks (519 of the 906 behaviors:
238 good behaviors and 281 issues) and asks the judge, in one call, to
cluster them into a MECE rubric set. Top attempts yield 238 good
behaviors and 59 issues, and bottom attempts 53 good behaviors and 281
issues; stage two drops the 112 behaviors that run against their
attempt’s outcome, the 259 behaviors of middle attempts, and the 16
behaviors of valid attempts that Kaggle did not score.

#### Coverage of dropped behaviors.

To test whether the stage-two filter discards behaviors that would form
new rubrics, we ask the same judge to assign each of the 387 dropped
behaviors to the one discovered rubric it instantiates, or to none if no
rubric clearly covers it, with the prompt below. Behaviors are sent in
batches of about 30, each with its kind, lens, text, and up to two
evidence quotes cut to 160 characters; the 17 rubrics are given by name
and one-sentence description, and sampling uses temperature 0. As a
baseline, we apply the same prompt to 60 randomly sampled kept
behaviors. The judge assigns 378 of the 387 dropped behaviors (97.7%) to
a rubric, against 59 of the 60 kept behaviors (98.3%). The nine
unassigned behaviors are mostly isolated, low-severity cases, such as a
wasted file operation; the largest group, two behaviors in which the
final model was trained on a small subsample of the data, is close to
Timeout-Aware Experiment Design.

## Appendix F DataPRM Baseline

DataPRM [Qiu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12) is a generative process reward
model for agentic data analysis. For each step of a trajectory it
reasons about the step, writes and executes Python code against the task
files to check it, and outputs a ternary score (1 for a correct step,
0.5 for minor issues, 0 for a fatal error) with a one-sentence summary.
Its authors use it for best-of-$`N`$ selection and as a reward in
reinforcement learning. We use the released checkpoint trained on
ScienceAgentBench (zjunlp/DataPRM-ScienceAgentBench, 4B parameters,
fine-tuned from Qwen3-4B-Instruct), the closer of the two released
checkpoints to model-building tasks; the other is trained on DABStep
question answering. We serve it with vLLM on one A100 GPU.

#### Integration.

DataPRM replaces the PRA and every other setting is that of AdaPRA: the
base agent, harness, five-attempt protocol, cadence ($`c{=}10`$), review
on finish, finish refinement, and feedback channel
(Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model inference settings. ‣ Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The condition therefore isolates the supervisor and compares a generic
step-level reward model with rubric-based supervision under identical
conditions. At each invocation DataPRM verifies, in order, each agent
turn taken since the previous invocation. One turn (the agent’s action
and its output) is one step, which matches DataPRM’s native split of a
trajectory into paragraphs, and each step is judged with all earlier
steps and DataPRM’s own earlier verifications as history. We keep the
released judge prompt verbatim and the released inference settings: up
to 10 reasoning and execution rounds per step, 8,192 generated tokens
per round, execution outputs truncated to 8,192 characters, a 30 s limit
per code execution, cumulative re-execution of earlier successful code
within a step, and sampling at temperature 0.7, top-$`p`$ 0.9, and
top-$`k`$ 20. An invocation returns FAIL if any verified step scores 0,
WARN if any scores 0.5, and PASS otherwise. The summaries of steps
scoring 0 or 0.5 are injected into the agent’s conversation, and a FAIL
at finish triggers the same refinement round as a PRA FAIL.

#### Adaptations to online supervision.

DataPRM is released for offline scoring of complete trajectories, and
running it during an attempt requires five changes. (1) At each
invocation it scores the steps taken since the previous invocation,
because online feedback must arrive before the attempt ends. (2)
Offline, DataPRM re-executes all of the agent’s earlier code to rebuild
the workspace before verifying a step. Our agents train models for up to
hours per attempt, which makes re-execution infeasible, so DataPRM’s
code instead runs in a writable directory linked to the agent’s live
workspace and the task data, with the agent’s workspace paths mapped
onto it; the code can therefore read every file the agent has produced.
(3) The ScienceAgentBench checkpoint was trained with a query_image
tool. We keep the tool’s description in the prompt to match the training
distribution, but no vision model is served, so a call returns a message
that the tool is unavailable; DSPredict-Easy is tabular, so the tool is
rarely relevant. (4) Each earlier step in the history is clipped to
2,000 characters and the current step to 12,000, and the oldest history
steps are dropped, so that each prompt fits the 24K-token context used
in training. (5) Each step shows the agent’s reasoning, its action in
full (the command, the text of a recorded thought, or the path and
contents of a file it writes), and the action’s output.

#### Behavior.

Over its 1,590 invocations on DSPredict-Easy, DataPRM verifies a median
of 10 steps per invocation in a median of 126 s. It returns FAIL on 43%
of invocations, WARN on 32%, and PASS on 24%, and it scores 10% of the
verified steps 0. Most zero scores flag an error in the step’s code or
analysis, such as a script that fails to run, a reference to a file that
does not exist, or a mismatch between the stated plan and the code, and
others penalize an approach that the agent already tried in an earlier
attempt.

## Appendix G Rubric and Principle Reward Models

Recent work has explored rubrics, checklists, and natural-language
principles as more flexible reward specifications than scalar preference
labels. Rubric-supervised critics learn dense behavioral features from
sparse real-world outcomes, showing that structured rubric labels can
improve reward modeling and test-time selection [Wang et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib17). Rubrics as Rewards uses structured rubric criteria
as reward signals for reinforcement learning beyond domains with easily
verifiable answers [Gunjal et al. (2025)](#bib.bib2). Checklist-based
approaches similarly decompose instructions into explicit criteria that
can be judged or verified to produce reward signals [Viswanathan et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib16). Most closely, RewardAnything introduces
principle-following reward models and RABench to test whether reward
models can follow dynamically provided natural-language principles and
generalize to novel principles without retraining [Yu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib21). A related reframing appears in MetaLint, which
casts code linting as instruction following over user-specified best
practices instead of classification over a fixed set of issue types
[Naik et al. (2025)](#bib.bib9). Like these principle-following models,
the PRA receives its rubrics as input instead of learning them in
training. Unlike them, it judges long-horizon agent trajectories and the
artifacts they produce instead of a single final response, and it can
revise the rubrics it receives.

## Appendix H Selection-Policy Analysis

Reporting the best attempt assumes that it can be identified after the
fact, which is not possible in deployment.
Tables [6](#A8.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix H Selection-Policy Analysis ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
and
[7](#A8.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix H Selection-Policy Analysis ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
report the leaderboard percentile under four ways of choosing one
attempt per task: the first attempt, the last attempt, the mean over
scored attempts, which is the expected result of choosing an attempt at
random, and the best attempt. The last attempt is the natural deployment
choice for a sequential run in a shared workspace, since each attempt
can build on the ones before it.

On DSPredict-Easy the last attempt improves on the first by 4.5 points
without supervision and by 6.5 points with AdaPRA, whose last attempt
(62.9) comes within 6.1 points of its best-attempt score (69.0). On
DSPredict-Hard the last attempt improves on the first under every
condition. AdaPRA has the highest mean and best-attempt percentiles
(32.1 and 36.1), and its last attempt (30.2) is within 0.2 points of the
highest last-attempt score ($`-`$PRA, 30.4).

## Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision

We test whether each supervised condition improves over the harness
alone
(Tables [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
and [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
and we report the same tests for AdaPRA against each of its two
ablations in the text. The unit of analysis is the task, and paired
differences $`d_{i}=\text{condition}_{i}-\text{reference}_{i}`$ cancel
differences in task difficulty. The primary test is a one-sided paired
permutation test on the mean difference $`\bar{d}`$. Under the null
hypothesis that the two conditions are exchangeable within each task,
each $`d_{i}`$ is equally likely to take either sign, so we compare the
observed $`\bar{d}`$ with its distribution under $`200{,}000`$ random
sign flips of the $`d_{i}`$. Unlike the sign test, this test uses the
magnitude of each difference, and unlike the Wilcoxon signed-rank test,
it tests the mean difference that we report without assuming that the
differences are symmetric. We also report the one-sided sign test, the
one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and a nested bootstrap 95%
confidence interval, which resamples tasks with replacement and then
attempts within each task, so the interval includes variation across
attempts. Both metrics of
Tables [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
and
[2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
are tested: the best attempt and the mean over a task’s valid attempts.
Percentiles use the private leaderboard where one exists and the public
leaderboard otherwise.

On DSPredict-Easy ($`n=38`$,
Table [8](#A9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
AdaPRA has the largest gains over the harness alone on both metrics
(best attempt $`+8.2`$, $`p<0.001`$, CI $`[+4.4,+14.4]`$; per attempt
$`+9.7`$, $`p<0.001`$). The gains of $`-`$adaptive rubrics are
significant on both metrics (best attempt $`+6.5`$, $`p=0.017`$; per
attempt $`+7.5`$, $`p=0.008`$). The best-attempt gain of $`-`$PRA is not
significant ($`+2.2`$, $`p=0.273`$), but its per-attempt gain is
($`+6.6`$, $`p=0.009`$). Compared directly on the best attempt, AdaPRA
outperforms $`-`$PRA ($`+6.0`$; 23 wins, 15 losses; $`p=0.012`$), while
its gain over $`-`$adaptive rubrics is not significant ($`+1.7`$; 22
wins, 16 losses; $`p=0.147`$).

On DSPredict-Hard ($`n=54`$,
Table [9](#A9.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix I Paired Significance of Process Supervision ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
every supervised condition improves significantly over the harness alone
on both metrics, and AdaPRA has the largest gains (best attempt
$`+10.6`$, $`p<0.001`$, CI $`[+5.3,+16.2]`$; per attempt $`+7.8`$,
$`p=0.001`$, CI $`[+2.8,+13.0]`$). The gains of $`-`$PRA are significant
on both metrics (best attempt $`+6.3`$, $`p=0.009`$; per attempt
$`+6.7`$, $`p<0.001`$), as are those of $`-`$adaptive rubrics (best
attempt $`+6.3`$, $`p=0.007`$; per attempt $`+5.5`$, $`p=0.005`$).
Compared directly on the best attempt, AdaPRA outperforms $`-`$adaptive
rubrics ($`+4.3`$; 32 wins, 13 losses; $`p=0.024`$), so rubric
adaptation adds to code execution on the held-out benchmark. Its gain
over $`-`$PRA ($`+4.3`$; 29 wins, 18 losses) is not significant
($`p=0.077`$). Per attempt, neither direct difference is significant
($`+2.3`$, $`p=0.138`$; $`+1.1`$, $`p=0.358`$).

Figure 3: Offline rubric discovery. The base agent’s attempts on each

clusters the good behaviors of top attempts and the issues of bottom

behaviors as evidence for the same rubric (prompts and settings in
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ Appendix E Prompts ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

## Appendix J Seed Rubrics

Table [10](#A10.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
lists the 19 seed rubrics that initialize every rubric store
(§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Rubric Discovery ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
and
Tables [11](#A10.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")–[15](#A10.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
give their full natural-language definitions. The PRA receives each
rubric as its one-sentence definition followed by its four labels
(satisfied, violated, not applicable, insufficient evidence) and a note
stating the rubric’s evidence source, which is phrased as a
recommendation so that the PRA may use either kind of evidence.
Seventeen rubrics come from offline discovery on harness-only
DSPredict-Easy runs. Four of them are restated to reason over all
earlier attempts on the task, and two further rubrics are hand-curated.
Stage one mines each attempt independently, so it cannot surface
failures that appear only across attempts, such as later attempts
converging on the same solution; the two hand-curated rubrics target
these failures. They account for 11–17% of rubric failures across the
supervised runs, and they are the only failing rubrics in 1–3% of
reviews that report a failure. Six rubrics refer to the transcripts of
earlier attempts, which the PRA reads on demand
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Process Reward Agent ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The rubric names and definitions are reproduced verbatim; “best-of-N” in
them refers to the $`N`$ sequential attempts on a task, of which the
best is scored.

_Discovered, restated_ rubrics were restated to judge the current

target cross-attempt failures. _Support_: number of the 519 behaviors

| Rubric and definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Satisfied if                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Violated if                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Not applicable / insufficient evidence if                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Persistent CV Score Registry (cv_score_registry). Whether the agent maintains a persistent cv_scores.json (or equivalent) updated after every experiment to enable objective cross-model comparison.                                         | A machine-readable file (e.g., cv_scores.json) exists in the workspace containing CV scores for every trained model/ensemble, updated consistently throughout the run, and the agent uses it to identify the best model at submission time.                                                                                                    | No such registry exists, or it is missing entries for major experiments, or it is overwritten per-run rather than accumulated, preventing reliable comparison across all experiments.                                                                                                    | _N/A:_ Only a single model was ever trained and no comparison was needed. _Insufficient:_ The workspace files are not visible and the trajectory does not mention CV score tracking. |
| Best-CV Model Submission Selection (best_model_submission_selection). Whether the agent explicitly selects and submits the model with the best CV score rather than whatever was most recently trained or written to disk.                   | The final /submission/submission.csv is verifiably sourced from the model/experiment with the highest CV score in the registry, and the agent explicitly checked the registry before writing the final submission.                                                                                                                             | The submission corresponds to a later, lower-CV experiment that overwrote the best model’s output, or the agent selected the most-recent model without checking CV scores.                                                                                                               | _N/A:_ Only one model was trained so no selection was needed. _Insufficient:_ It cannot be determined which model’s predictions are in the submission file.                          |
| Valid Cross-Validation Methodology (valid_cv_methodology). Whether the agent uses a proper out-of-fold or held-out cross-validation scheme that produces honest, unbiased CV score estimates.                                                | All reported CV scores are computed using held-out fold predictions (OOF) that were not used during model fitting, with an appropriate split strategy for the task (stratified for classification, time-based for time series).                                                                                                                | Any CV score in cv_scores.json is computed by evaluating a model on the same data it was trained on (in-sample), or ensemble weights are searched using the same OOF data without a secondary holdout, or the CV scheme is wrong for the task type (e.g., random KFold for time series). | _N/A:_ No model training or CV was performed. _Insufficient:_ The training code is not visible and CV methodology cannot be inferred from outputs.                                   |
| Suspicious CV Score Investigation (suspicious_cv_score_investigation). Whether the agent investigates and correctly handles CV scores that are suspiciously better than all other models (a signal of data leakage or in-sample evaluation). | When a model’s CV score is substantially better than all others ($`>`$ 20% relative improvement with no architectural explanation), the agent diagnoses whether it is legitimate or an artifact of leakage/in-sample evaluation, and either discards the model or confirms correctness with a separate holdout before using it for submission. | An obviously inflated CV score (e.g., perfect 1.0 AUC, RMSE 10x better than all others, correlation 0.96 with training labels) is accepted as valid, recorded in cv_scores.json, and used for submission or downstream ensembling without investigation.                                 | _N/A:_ No suspiciously anomalous CV scores appeared during the run. _Insufficient:_ CV score values are not visible in the trajectory or workspace.                                  |
| Metric Calculation Bug Detection (metric_bug_detection). Whether the agent detects and corrects bugs in metric calculation code before reporting or acting on CV scores.                                                                     | When a CV score appears implausibly low or inconsistent with prior results (e.g., RMSLE of 0.01 when all prior models score ~0.13), the agent identifies and fixes the root cause in the metric code before using the score for model selection.                                                                                               | An obviously buggy metric (double log-transform, wrong target, train-set RMSE) produces a clearly impossible CV score that the agent reports as valid and uses for multiple turns before catching it (if ever).                                                                          | _N/A:_ No metric bugs occurred and all CV scores were plausible. _Insufficient:_ The metric calculation code is not visible.                                                         |

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Satisfied if | Model Diversity and Ensembling (model_diversity_and_ensembling). Whether the agent trains at least two distinct model families and combines them via ensemble or stacking, and whether model-family coverage across the best-of-N attempts is diverse rather than duplicated. _Context:_ This is a best-of-N run (N=n_attempts); the submitted result is the MAX over attempts, so what matters is the diversity of the WHOLE beam, not just this attempt. Read the accumulated prior-attempt transcripts (traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt in /reviewer/) and cv_scores.json to see which model families the earlier attempts already covered.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | The workspace contains trained models from at least two distinct families (e.g., LightGBM + XGBoost, or GBDT + neural net), their OOF predictions are combined via weighted averaging or stacking with the ensemble CV compared against individual models, AND – across attempts – the best-of-N beam is not collapsing onto one family (i.e., this attempt either adds a family/architecture the beam has not tried or is early enough that convergence is not yet a concern).                   | Only one model family was trained, or models from multiple families were trained but never combined, or an ensemble combined weak+strong models in a way that degraded performance (e.g., blending with a model 2.5pp weaker), OR this attempt is re-training essentially the same model families/ensemble the prior attempts already built (duplicating the beam) when a distinct family could have been tried. | _N/A:_ The competition or task type makes single-model submission standard (e.g., data-centric competition where model is fixed), or fewer than two attempts have run so cross-attempt diversity cannot yet be assessed. _Insufficient:_ Training scripts and the prior-attempt transcripts are not visible. |
| Hyperparameter Tuning Beyond Defaults (hyperparameter_tuning). Whether the agent performs at least one principled hyperparameter search beyond default settings for the primary model family – while recognizing when tuning has already been exhausted in earlier best-of-N attempts. _Context:_ This is a best-of-N run (N=n_attempts). Before scoring, consult the accumulated prior-attempt transcripts (traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt in /reviewer/) and cv_scores.json to see whether hyperparameter search was ALREADY done in an earlier attempt and what it yielded.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | EITHER the workspace contains at least one training script or cv_scores.json entry showing a model trained with non-default hyperparameters (e.g., num_leaves != 31, learning_rate != 0.05, or a grid/random/Optuna search) with the tuned CV compared against baseline, OR the agent correctly recognizes that prior attempts already tuned this family to saturation (no meaningful CV gain) and therefore spends its budget elsewhere (new family, features, diversity) rather than re-tuning. | The primary model uses default/near-default hyperparameters (num_leaves=31, max_depth=6, lr=0.05) with no documented search AND no earlier attempt tuned it either, OR a ’tuned’ variant produced CV identical to baseline. Do NOT reward re-running a hyperparameter search that a prior attempt already showed to be saturated – that is over-optimization, not diligence.                                     | _N/A:_ The task is data-centric (fixed model) or the budget was trivially small. _Insufficient:_ Hyperparameter values are not visible in training scripts, the registry, or the prior-attempt transcripts.                                                                                                  |
| Hedging Across Best-of-N With Diverse Model Classes (single_model_class_hedging). Whether the best-of-N attempts hedge across DIFFERENT modeling classes rather than converging on the same solution near finish – using the max-over-N structure to try a distinct approach (even a second-best one) instead of duplicating the leading attempt. _Context:_ This is a best-of-N run (N=n_attempts) and the SUBMITTED result is the MAX over attempts, so a genuinely different modeling class that ends up second-best costs nothing, while a duplicate of an existing attempt wastes one of the N shots. Judge this ACROSS attempts using the accumulated prior-attempt transcripts (traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt in /reviewer/), the final submissions / cached test predictions, and cv_scores.json. Only assess once enough attempts exist to see convergence (typically attempt index $`\geq`$ 2). | The attempts hedge across distinct modeling classes/architectures (e.g., GBDT ensemble in one, a neural net or a linear/kernel model or a very different feature representation in another), so the best-of-N beam covers meaningfully different solutions rather than one repeated recipe.                                                                                                                                                                                                       | More than two of the attempts converge near finish on essentially the same solution – same model family and features, near-identical final predictions or CV, often reusing the same cached OOF/test preds – instead of at least one attempt deliberately trying a different modeling class to exploit best-of-N.                                                                                                | _N/A:_ Fewer than three attempts have completed, or the task is data-centric / single-model by nature so diversifying the model class is not meaningful. _Insufficient:_ The final solutions of the prior attempts cannot be compared from the transcripts, submissions, or registry.                        |

| Training Objective–Metric Alignment (metric_objective_alignment). Whether the agent aligns the model’s training objective or target transformation with the competition evaluation metric.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | The training loss or target transformation matches the evaluation metric (e.g., log1p target for RMSLE, MAE objective for MedAE, stratified splits for imbalanced AUC, ordinal-aware loss for QWK).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Models are trained with a mismatched objective (e.g., RMSE on raw target for an RMSLE competition, MSE for QWK, no log transform for RMSLE), as evidenced in training scripts or cv_scores.json metadata.                                                                                                                  | _N/A:_ The competition metric is accuracy or AUC and any standard classification objective is acceptable. _Insufficient:_ Training scripts are not visible and metric alignment cannot be inferred.                            |
| Domain-Appropriate Preprocessing (domain_appropriate_preprocessing). Whether the agent applies preprocessing steps appropriate to the model type and task (avoiding scaling before tree models, using correct imputation, appropriate CV splits).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Preprocessing choices are appropriate: no feature scaling before tree-based models, correct imputation strategy for the target distribution, and CV split type matches the task (stratified for imbalanced classification, time-based for time series).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | StandardScaler is applied before LightGBM/XGBoost/CatBoost, target NaN values are imputed with 0 for a forecasting task, or random KFold is used for a time-series problem where temporal leakage would inflate CV scores.                                                                                                 | _N/A:_ Only linear models were used (where scaling is appropriate) or there were no categorical/missing-value features. _Insufficient:_ Preprocessing code is not visible.                                                     |
| Feature Engineering Investment (feature_engineering_investment). Whether the agent invests in at least one round of principled feature engineering beyond raw input columns, accounting for feature work already done in earlier best-of-N attempts. _Context:_ This is a best-of-N run (N=n_attempts). Consult the accumulated prior-attempt transcripts (traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt in /reviewer/), features.py/preprocess.py in the persistent workspace, and cv_scores.json to see what feature engineering earlier attempts already tried and whether it helped. | EITHER the workspace contains a feature-engineering script/module adding at least 3 non-trivial derived features (interactions, target encodings, lag features, domain transforms) with a CV comparison showing improvement over the raw-feature baseline, OR this attempt sensibly builds on / diverges from the feature work prior attempts established (e.g., a prior attempt found feature set A helped, so this attempt reuses A and explores a different modeling axis, or a prior attempt found FE gave no lift so this attempt reasonably invests its budget elsewhere). | All training scripts use only raw input columns (label-encoding/fillna only) and NO attempt – this one or an earlier one – engineered features despite a non-trivial feature space; OR this attempt merely re-derives the exact same features a prior attempt already built and validated, adding nothing new to the beam. | _N/A:_ The competition is data-centric (fixed model) or the feature space is already maximal (e.g., pre-extracted embeddings). _Insufficient:_ Feature-engineering code and the prior-attempt transcripts cannot be inspected. |
