Whether the agent detects when a subsequent experiment produces a CV regression and explicitly reverts the submission to the best-validated model.       | The agent detects (via cv_scores.json comparison or file inspection) that the current submission.csv corresponds to a worse model than a previously computed best, and explicitly restores the best model’s predictions to /submission/submission.csv before finishing. | The final submission reflects a worse model because the agent did not check for regressions, or detected a regression but failed to revert before finishing.                                                                          | _N/A:_ Only one model was trained, making regression impossible. _Insufficient:_ It cannot be determined whether a regression occurred or was addressed.                           |
| Avoiding Repeated Identical Crashes (no_repeated_identical_crashes). Whether the agent diagnoses and fixes the root cause of a crash rather than repeatedly re-running the same failing code.                                  | When a script crashes, the agent identifies the root cause, applies a fix, and the same error does not recur more than once after the fix.                                                                                                                              | The same error (same exception type and cause, e.g., wrong keyword argument, dtype mismatch, array shape error) appears three or more times across successive turns, indicating the agent is re-running without root-cause diagnosis. | _N/A:_ No crashes occurred during the trajectory. _Insufficient:_ Error messages and fix attempts are not visible in the transcript.                                               |

| Avoiding Churn Without Pivoting (no_churn_without_pivot). Whether the agent recognizes when an experimental axis has plateaued – WITHIN this attempt or ACROSS the best-of-N attempts – and pivots to a substantively different approach rather than repeating near-identical experiments. _Context:_ This is a best-of-N run (N=n_attempts). Assess churn at BOTH scales, using the accumulated prior-attempt transcripts (traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt in /reviewer/), cv_scores.json, and the submission ledger to reconstruct what earlier attempts already tried.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Within the attempt, after 2-3 consecutive experiments on the same axis (weight search, seed sweep) yield no meaningful CV improvement ($`<`$ 0.001 relative) the agent pivots to a different approach (new model family, feature engineering, different stacking architecture); AND, across attempts, this attempt does not merely repeat an axis a prior attempt already saturated – it explores something the beam has not tried. | EITHER five or more consecutive experiments within the attempt make no substantive change and no meaningful CV gain (nearly identical cv_scores.json entries or repeated ’No improvement found’), OR this attempt re-runs the same saturated axis a prior attempt already exhausted (e.g., yet another ensemble-weight sweep on the same cached OOF predictions) instead of pivoting – the classic best-of-N beam collapse where multiple attempts converge on the same solution. | _N/A:_ The agent only ran one or two experiments total and no prior attempt covered this axis. _Insufficient:_ The number and variety of experiments cannot be determined from the transcript or the prior-attempt transcripts are unavailable.                                          |
| Valid Submission Before Finishing (no_premature_termination). Whether the agent ensures a valid, complete submission file exists at /submission/submission.csv before concluding the attempt.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | At the time of finish, /submission/submission.csv exists, is a valid CSV with the correct target column and row count matching the test set, and contains non-trivial (non-constant, non-NaN) predictions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | finish is called before any valid submission is written, or the submission file is empty, binary-corrupted, or contains wrong-competition predictions that make it invalid for the actual leaderboard.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | _N/A:_ The attempt is still in progress and no finish was called. _Insufficient:_ The submission file contents cannot be verified.                                                                                                                                                       |
| Timeout-Aware Experiment Design (timeout_aware_experiment_design). Whether the agent designs experiments to complete within available time budgets, using prototyping or parameter adjustment rather than launching full training jobs that are repeatedly killed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Before launching expensive training jobs (large datasets, many folds, many boosting rounds), the agent either runs a single-fold prototype to estimate runtime, or explicitly limits parameters (sample size, n_folds, n_estimators) to fit within the time budget – and no major training job is killed before saving results.                                                                                                     | Two or more training scripts are interrupted with Ctrl-C or timeout before saving any useful predictions or CV scores, indicating the agent launched jobs without verifying they would complete.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | _N/A:_ All training jobs completed successfully without interruption. _Insufficient:_ Job runtimes and completion status are not visible in the transcript.                                                                                                                              |
| Over-Optimization Without Significant Gains (over_optimization). Whether the agent avoids burning a disproportionate share of turns on hyperparameter tuning and ensemble-weight search that yields no statistically meaningful CV improvement, judged within the current attempt AND across the best-of-N attempts. _Context:_ This is a best-of-N run (N=n_attempts); the submitted result is the MAX over attempts, so grinding for a 4th-decimal CV gain rarely changes the outcome while it burns budget that a different approach could use. ’Statistically meaningful’ means the CV gain exceeds the fold-to-fold noise: compare the improvement to cv_std in cv_scores.json (a rule of thumb: a gain smaller than ~0.25-0.5x cv_std, or $`<`$ ~0.001 relative when std is unavailable, is inside the noise). Use the accumulated prior-attempt transcripts (traj_a{attempt}\_t{turn}.txt in /reviewer/) and cv_scores.json to judge cumulative effort across attempts, not just this one. | Time spent on hyperparameter tuning / ensemble-weight search is proportionate – the agent stops optimizing an axis once gains fall within cv_std and redirects effort to a new model family, features, or a fresh attempt; the beam’s total tuning effort is not dominated by noise-level micro-optimization.                                                                                                                       | A large share of turns (roughly a third or more of the attempt, or the bulk of multiple attempts) goes to HPO or ensemble-weight tuning whose cumulative CV gain is within the noise floor ($`<`$ cv_std, e.g. AUC moving 0.8671$`\rightarrow`$0.8672 across 30+ turns, or repeated Optuna runs each landing within std of the last) – effort that best-of-N makes almost worthless.                                                                                              | _N/A:_ The agent did little or no hyperparameter/ensemble tuning, or tuning produced clearly meaningful ($`>`$ cv_std) gains. _Insufficient:_ cv_std / CV deltas or the turn-level breakdown of effort cannot be recovered from the transcript, workspace, or prior-attempt transcripts. |

## Appendix K Seed Rubric Failures Across Benchmarks

Table [16](#A11.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Appendix K Seed Rubric Failures Across Benchmarks ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
compares the 19 seed rubrics
(Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J Seed Rubrics ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
in the $`-`$adaptive rubrics runs on both benchmarks. Both runs score
the same rubrics at every review, so the rates are directly comparable.
A rubric fails in a review when it crosses the injection thresholds
(Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model inference settings. ‣ Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The analysis covers 190 DSPredict-Easy attempts and 270 DSPredict-Hard
attempts. Across the 19 rubrics, Spearman correlations between
benchmarks are $`\rho=0.66`$ ($`p=0.002`$) for attempt failure rate and
$`\rho=0.91`$ ($`p<10^{-7}`$) for mean importance.

#### Examples of transferred rubrics.

Table [17](#A11.T17 "Table 17 ‣ Examples of transferred rubrics. ‣ Appendix K Seed Rubric Failures Across Benchmarks ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
pairs seven failures that the PRA flagged on non-tabular DSPredict-Hard
tasks with the same rubric failing on a tabular DSPredict-Easy task.
Each example comes from the frozen-rubric run, so the rubric text is
exactly as discovered on DSPredict-Easy. We count a flag as _resolved_
when the PRA scores a rubric at importance $`\geq 0.6`$ and success
probability $`\leq 0.2`$ at one review, and at success probability
$`\geq 0.7`$ at a later review of the same attempt; for every example in
the table we read the later rationale to confirm that the agent fixed
the issue. Across the DSPredict-Hard frozen-rubric run, 685 of 1,277
flags (54%) are resolved within the attempt, on 53 of the 54 tasks.
Resolution rates are highest for rubrics that check the pipeline
(submission integrity 83%, regression detection 82%, best-model
selection 79%, metric bugs 67%, valid cross-validation 55%) and lowest
for the simplicity-bias rubrics (model diversity 16%, single-model-class
hedging 22%, pivoting when experiments stall 28%). Flagged pipeline
errors are usually fixed within the attempt, while flagged strategy
problems change the agent’s behavior less often.

## Appendix L Rubric Store Operations

Figure [4](#A12.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
counts the operations that the PRA applies to each task’s rubric store
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Adaptive Rubrics ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"))
in AdaPRA and its $`-`$PRA ablation, taken from the operation log of
each store. Adaptation consists almost entirely of additions. Across the
four runs the PRA adds 177 rubrics, updates one, and retires none.
Between 81% and 94% of additions occur in the first two attempts, so
later attempts are reviewed against a largely stable store. The $`-`$PRA
ablation adds rubrics at a similar rate (0.76 vs. 0.84 per task on
DSPredict-Easy and 1.10 vs. 1.21 on DSPredict-Hard), so removing code
execution does not reduce how often the store is edited.

ablation. (a) Operations by type, with raw counts above the bars. (b)
Additions by the attempt in which they occur. Rates are over tasks with

and 49 tasks, for AdaPRA and $`-`$PRA).

breaks these operations down by run and attempt, and
Figure [6](#A12.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
shows how many rubrics each task’s store gains. With code execution the
PRA adds at least one rubric on 79% of DSPredict-Hard tasks, compared
with 55% for $`-`$PRA, while on DSPredict-Easy the shares are 51% and
63%.
Table [18](#A12.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix L Rubric Store Operations ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
groups the added rubrics by what they check, a grouping we assigned by
reading each rubric. Prediction-sanity rubrics, which compute statistics
of the agent’s predictions such as their dispersion relative to the
target, account for 35% (DSPredict-Easy) and 19% (DSPredict-Hard) of
additions with code execution and 3% and 7% without it, and the $`-`$PRA
ablation instead adds mostly train–test and submission consistency
rubrics (41% and 44%).

## Appendix M Example PRA Feedback

This appendix reproduces PRA feedback from the AdaPRA runs on
DSPredict-Easy and DSPredict-Hard, with the agent’s response and the
leaderboard outcome of the attempt. Each PRA box shows the failed
rubrics as the agent received them
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Process Reward Agent ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
Each agent box shows the agent’s subsequent actions, with each step
labeled by turn and long passages abridged as “\[…\]”. Attempts are

the competition has only a public one, and CV denotes the agent’s local

#### Execution grounding exposes an in-sample calibration gain.

In _Feature Imputation with a Heat Flux Dataset_, the agent fitted
isotonic regression on its full set of XGBoost out-of-fold predictions,
scored it on the same rows, and submitted it because the RMSE fell from
0.073994 to 0.073592. The PRA reran the calibration under nested
cross-validation and found an RMSE of 0.074386, worse than the
uncalibrated model. It then added a task-specific rubric,
calibration_not_insample, with a natural-language definition and a check
script (calibration_insample_check.py) that fits the calibrator on four
folds and scores the fifth
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Adaptive Rubrics ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
The agent reverted the submission in the next two turns and finished the
attempt with a Ridge stack of LightGBM, XGBoost, and CatBoost (CV
0.073815). The private percentile rose from 49.7 in attempt 1 to 62.2 in
attempt 2, while the public percentile was unchanged (52.4 and 52.0).

#### A task-specific rubric bounds a weak formulation before it runs.

In the _TGS Salt Identification Challenge_, the agent began attempt 1 by
training logistic regression on global image statistics to predict
whether an image contains salt, and planned to submit an all-salt or
all-empty mask per image. Before this model produced a score, the PRA
computed the salt fill fraction of every training mask and derived that
even a perfect image-level classifier is capped at 0.52 mean average
precision under the competition’s IoU thresholds. It recorded this bound
as a new rubric, pixel_segmentation_vs_image_classification, backed by
check_segmentation_approach.py. The agent replaced the classifier with a
U-Net trained with per-pixel cross-entropy within five turns. The rubric
passed in all 21 subsequent reviews recorded for the task, which
confirmed from the submitted run-length encodings that every attempt
predicted image-specific masks. Two further rubrics added in attempt 1
had a similar lasting effect. One of them
(oof_is_fold_predictions_not_full_model) caught at turn 100 that the
saved out-of-fold array came from the model refit on all data, since it
reproduced a score of 0.1654 against a reported fold CV of 0.5005. Its
check then verified every later CV to within $`10^{-4}`$. Attempt 1
itself, with a five-epoch U-Net, reached a private percentile of only
10.1. Later attempts built on its pipeline with ResNet encoders, reached
CV above 0.70, and scored private percentiles of 34.3 to 36.6.

#### The PRA prevents a revert caused by the agent’s own diagnostic bug.

In _Multi-Class Prediction of Obesity Risk_, attempts 1 and 2 had
trained only gradient-boosted trees, and in attempt 3 the score registry
had fallen out of sync with the prediction files. The current submission
came from XGBoost with an out-of-fold accuracy of 0.909240, but the
agent’s own accuracy script compared class labels against column names
carrying a prob\_ prefix and reported XGBoost as 0.000000. The PRA
reproduced the correct accuracy from the saved predictions, located the
prefix bug, and warned the agent against reverting to the weaker
CatBoost model. The agent applied the one-line fix, obtained 0.909240,
and corrected the registry within four turns. It followed the PRA’s
diversification requests by training an MLP, which timed out, and a
logistic regression (CV 0.8569), which the PRA’s review at turn 50 found
would lower accuracy in a hard vote with XGBoost. The final submission
was a 0.9/0.1 soft vote of XGBoost and CatBoost with CV 0.910059, a
weighting the PRA had computed from the cached predictions at turn 60.
The private percentile rose from 49.4 in attempt 2 to 73.3 in attempt 3.

#### The finish gate catches a CV that the submission does not reproduce.

In _Digit Recognizer_, the agent called finish at turn 44 with a
ResNet-18 and a reported CV of 0.9922. At the finish review, the PRA
recomputed accuracy from the saved out-of-fold predictions (0.9899) and
traced the gap to the training script. The script recorded best-epoch
validation accuracy as the CV score but generated out-of-fold and test
predictions from the last-epoch weights, and it never reloaded the
best-epoch checkpoints. The failed review returned the attempt to the
agent for its one refinement round
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Process Reward Agent ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
in which the agent reloaded the checkpoints, retrained, and finished
with an out-of-fold accuracy of 0.9912 that matched the reported score.
The attempt reached a public percentile of 87.0 (accuracy 0.99482; the
competition has no private leaderboard), up from 73.3 for attempt 4 (a
three-layer CNN) and 21.7 to 22.1 for attempts 1 to 3. The gain over
attempt 4 also reflects the change of architecture, so it cannot be
attributed to the fix alone. Earlier in the same attempt (turn 20), the
PRA had found that the submission file matched the XGBoost predictions
row for row while the CNN held the best CV, and the agent restored the
CNN submission in the next turn.

#### Cross-attempt review breaks a collapsed beam.

In _Titanic_, all four earlier attempts submitted the same CatBoost
model (CV 0.8552), and the last three of them were identical on all 418
test rows. At turn 10 of the final attempt, the PRA read the earlier
attempts’ trajectories and prediction files, reported the collapse, and
quantified how far the cached predictions of other model families
departed from CatBoost (26 to 41 of 418 rows). The agent built a
weighted vote over the cached test predictions that differed from
CatBoost on 26 rows. The public accuracy rose from 0.77033 to 0.77511
and the public percentile from 32.8 to 52.4 (the competition has no
private leaderboard). The agent spent six turns on an ensemble-weight
search, which the PRA had advised against, and it never computed an
out-of-fold score for the ensemble. Its registry entry reuses the
CatBoost value as a proxy. The PRA raised this at later reviews and at
the finish gate, and the attempt ended with the issue unresolved.

#### Diversity feedback breaks a duplicated baseline, and an executed check validates the ensemble.

In _Regression of Used Car Prices_, attempts 1 and 2 submitted the same
LightGBM baseline (CV RMSE 77,242.70, private percentile 9.7). At turn
10 of attempt 3, the PRA failed both cross-attempt rubrics and the
model-diversity rubric. It reported that two of the five submissions
were identical and that every model that had completed training was a
LightGBM, XGBoost, or CatBoost variant. From the saved predictions it
also measured that the baseline’s predictions had 0.148 times the
standard deviation of the target. The agent first tried the suggested
CatBoost model with native categorical features, which exceeded its
300-second timeout, and then trained scikit-learn’s
HistGradientBoosting, the PRA’s other suggestion. Although this is also
a gradient-boosted tree model, it lowered CV to 73,209. After the
turn-20 review reported that the model still underpredicted expensive
cars, the agent added fold-isolated brand and model price encodings and
finished with CV 73,185 and a private percentile of 43.6, equal to the
best attempt of the harness-only run on this task. In attempt 4, the
agent submitted a near-equal-weight average of HistGradientBoosting,
LightGBM, and XGBoost without scoring it. At turn 31, the PRA estimated
the average’s CV at 75,876, worse than HistGradientBoosting alone
(73,174). It also found that the largest submitted prediction was \$145K
while the largest out-of-fold prediction was \$443K. The agent reverted
to HistGradientBoosting, saved out-of-fold predictions for each base
model, and trained a Ridge stack on them (CV 72,590 at turn 55). The
attempt reached a private percentile of 80.5.

#### Cross-attempt review adds an image model to a beam of feature-based models.

In the _Statoil/C-CORE Iceberg Classifier Challenge_, the agent
classified two-band $`75\times 75`$ radar images from hand-crafted band
statistics in its first three attempts, using logistic regression with a
random forest, a stack of the two, and CatBoost (CV log loss 0.303,
private percentile 21.8). Early in attempt 4 it wrote a CNN on the raw
pixels, found that TensorFlow was not installed, and returned to
stacking tree models on the same features. At turn 80, the PRA reported
that no attempt had trained a model on the images themselves and that
the current attempt’s stack had only matched attempt 1 (CV 0.3766). The
PRA, which labels attempts from A0, recommended a CNN for the final
attempt. The agent instead wrote a PyTorch CNN in the current attempt
(CV 0.344). At turn 100, the PRA found the agent retraining the CNN and
computed from the cached out-of-fold predictions that a 0.45/0.55 blend
of CatBoost and the CNN reaches 0.2407. The agent recomputed the blend,
recorded it in the score registry, and submitted it. The private
percentile rose from 21.8 in attempt 3 to 52.3. Attempt 5 reached a
lower CV (0.232) but a private percentile of only 3.7, so the task’s
best-of-5 result comes from attempt 4.

#### An added rubric can encode an unattainable target.

In _Regression with a Tabular Concrete Strength Dataset_, the PRA added
prediction_dispersion_health at turn 20 of attempt 1. The rubric fails
when the standard deviation of out-of-fold predictions is below 0.80 of
the target’s and tail errors exceed twice the mid-range error. For a
calibrated regressor, the ratio of these standard deviations equals the
square root of the explained variance. At the agent’s CV RMSE of about
12.1 against a target standard deviation of 16.4, this gives about 0.68,
the value the PRA measured, and meeting the 0.80 threshold would require
an RMSE near 9.8. The agent followed the suggested sample weighting,
which raised the ratio from 0.664 to 0.680 and worsened CV from 12.121
to 12.184. The weighted run also overwrote the saved out-of-fold
predictions, and a later review had to flag the overwrite before the
agent restored its best model. The rubric failed in every review of
attempts 1 and 2 after it was added, including the final review of
attempt 2, whose stacked ensemble reached the task’s best private
percentile of 90.6. The agent also tried a Huber objective and quantile
regression in later attempts, and the final reports of attempts 2 and 4
still list a standard-deviation ratio of about 0.67. Adaptation lets the
PRA write criteria that no seed rubric covers, and this example shows
that it can also write criteria that conflict with the metric. Such a
rubric consumes turns until the PRA retires it, and here it was never
retired.

#### Summary.

Across these examples, the most useful feedback comes from checks the
PRA executes. These include recomputing a score from saved predictions,
nesting a calibration step, bounding an approach analytically from the
training labels, and diffing submissions across attempts. Each such
check produced a specific number that the agent could verify in one or
two turns, and the agent adopted most such fixes within a few turns.
Rubrics added by the PRA are most valuable when they encode a verified
property of the task, such as the image-level accuracy ceiling in the
TGS Salt Identification Challenge or the fold provenance of saved
predictions, since those rubrics then serve as persistent checks for
later attempts. Feedback that asks for broader exploration is most
productive when an executed check follows it. In _Regression of Used Car
Prices_ and the _Iceberg Classifier Challenge_, diversity feedback moved
the agent off a single model family. A later check then decided how to
combine the new model with the old ones, either by estimating an
ensemble’s CV or by computing a blend weight from cached predictions.
Without such a check, as in _Titanic_, the agent complies with the
letter of the request (a diverse submission) but omits the validation
that would justify the choice. An added rubric whose threshold conflicts
with the metric can persist across attempts and absorb turns, which
motivates retiring rubrics that fail repeatedly without a corresponding
loss in CV.

## Appendix N PRA Cadence

Table [19](#A14.T19 "Table 19 ‣ Appendix N PRA Cadence ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
varies the number of agent turns $`c`$ between PRA invocations on
DSPredict-Easy with one attempt per task. Every cadence improves over
the harness alone. Invoking the PRA every 10 turns performs best, while
$`c{=}5`$ interrupts the agent more often and $`c{=}20`$ delays
feedback. We use $`c{=}10`$ on DSPredict-Easy and $`c{=}20`$ on
DSPredict-Hard, where longer attempts would make $`c{=}10`$ twice as
costly in PRA invocations
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Ablations ‣ 5 Results ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
At $`c{=}20`$ the PRA still improves on the harness alone on
DSPredict-Easy.

| Cadence             | Valid | Pct. | Median |
| ------------------- | ----- | ---- | ------ |
| Harness only        | 94.7  | 48.4 | 55.3   |
| $`c{=}5`$           | 100.0 | 52.7 | 60.5   |
| $`c{=}10`$ (AdaPRA) | 100.0 | 56.4 | 65.8   |
| $`c{=}20`$          | 100.0 | 49.9 | 57.9   |

Table 19: Single-attempt results on DSPredict-Easy as a function of the
PRA cadence $`c`$ (agent turns between PRA invocations). All rows use
the same seed rubrics and PRA model. $`c{=}10`$ is the default setting
of AdaPRA.

## Appendix O Alternative Base Agent

Table [20](#A15.T20 "Table 20 ‣ Appendix O Alternative Base Agent ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")
replaces Qwen3-Coder-Next with DeepSeek-V3.2 as the base agent on
DSPredict-Easy, with one attempt per task. Both conditions otherwise use
the DSPredict-Easy settings of
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Model inference settings. ‣ Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science"),
except that DeepSeek-V3.2 runs as a reasoning model, with high reasoning
effort and the provider’s default temperature
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Harness Implementation Details ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
and AdaPRA keeps the same PRA model, seed rubrics, and cadence
($`c{=}10`$). With a single attempt, a failed attempt cannot be offset
by a later one, so the comparison measures whether supervision improves
the attempt itself. AdaPRA raises the mean percentile by 7.8 points and
doubles the above-median rate. Over tasks it wins 25 times, loses 11
times, and ties twice (one-sided paired permutation test $`p=0.005`$;
sign test $`p=0.014`$; Wilcoxon signed-rank $`p=0.006`$).

| Method       | Valid | Pct. | Median |
| ------------ | ----- | ---- | ------ |
| Harness only | 97.4  | 36.9 | 23.7   |
| AdaPRA       | 100.0 | 44.7 | 47.4   |

Table 20: Single-attempt results on DSPredict-Easy with DeepSeek-V3.2 as
the base agent. Rates use the fixed denominator of 38 tasks. Neither
condition reaches a medal threshold.

## Appendix R Feedback Content in an Earlier Version

This appendix reports an observation from an early development version
of our system (whose rubrics, supervisor, and harness differ from those
of the final system). In this version the supervisor reported every
rubric to the agent, regardless of whether it passed or failed. Most
rubrics passed in almost every report
(Figure [7](#A18.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix R Feedback Content in an Earlier Version ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")),
so the reports consisted largely of positive feedback. We found that the
agent’s next action was similar whether or not a report contained a
failure, ostensibly because the suggested actions from failures were
being drowned out by the overwhelmingly positive feedback. This
observation led to our design choice to include only failed rubrics
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Problem Setup ‣ 3 Method ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).

Figure 7: Share of scores in which each rubric passed or failed in an
earlier version of the system, over scores with importance $`\geq 0.6`$
(Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Feedback Content in an Earlier Version ‣ AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science")).
